projectDetails.name: Project AKASRA Space
projectDetails.summary:
AKASRA SurfaceWatch — See Earth's Changes. Understand Their Impact.

Founded in Cambodia, AKASRA Space aims to make space technology more accessible and useful for solving real-world challenges.

For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I developed SurfaceWatch, an interactive prototype that makes synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations easier to explore and interpret. The application enables users to compare two radar scenes, visualize potential water and wetland changes, adjust detection thresholds, inspect individual pixels, and export results.

The prototype includes a preprocessing pipeline designed for NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV data. Its current demonstration uses clearly identified synthetic imagery; real NISAR observations and independent validation remain future steps.

SurfaceWatch demonstrates a pathway toward accessible Earth observation tools supporting environmental research, floodplain management, and climate resilience.

My longer-term vision is to help build Cambodia's capabilities in satellite intelligence, AI, research, and space technology commercialization.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem

Earth's surface is constantly changing through natural processes and human activities. Understanding these changes is essential for environmental management, climate resilience, and sustainable development. However, cloud cover can limit optical satellite observations, while interpreting satellite radar data often requires specialized expertise.

Our Solution

I developed AKASRA SurfaceWatch, an interactive, open-source prototype designed to make Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations more accessible and understandable.

The application enables users to:

Compare earlier and later radar observations through an interactive slider.

Visualize potential changes in water and wetland surfaces.

Adjust detection thresholds and investigate individual pixels.

Explore radar backscatter changes through simple visual indicators.

Export images and analytical summaries for further investigation.

How It Works

SurfaceWatch is designed around NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) data.

Its preprocessing workflow accepts two comparable geocoded radar layers, aligns them, converts calibrated radar backscatter power into decibels, and computes changes between observations.

A transparent detection method highlights candidate water-related changes. Users can adjust the analysis parameters to explore different patterns.

The current demonstration uses synthetic radar-like data. The application and its Python preprocessing pipeline have been tested with synthetic georeferenced rasters. Processing and validation of actual NISAR observations remain future development steps.

Tools and Technologies

The project uses HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, Python, NumPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Pillow, and python-pptx. NASA Earthdata and Alaska Satellite Facility technical resources informed its NISAR-compatible processing workflow.

Innovation and Impact

SurfaceWatch combines scientific transparency, intuitive visualization, and an accessible interface.

Rather than presenting radar observations as complex technical imagery, it helps users explore changes, understand analytical assumptions, and recognize the limitations of automated detection.

Future applications could include wetland monitoring, flood-impact research, agricultural intelligence, and climate adaptation.

The prototype is exploratory. It does not currently provide validated flood mapping, operational monitoring, or disaster forecasting.

Long-Term Vision

As the founder and sole member of AKASRA Space, I see this project as an initial step toward building Cambodia's capabilities in space technology, satellite intelligence, artificial intelligence, and applied research.

My ambition is to connect Cambodian talent with the global space innovation ecosystem and transform scientific knowledge into solutions that benefit communities, governments, and businesses.

We do not need to begin by building rockets. We can begin by building people, capabilities, and solutions that make space technology useful for humanity.

projectDetails.name: Project Kawachii
projectDetails.summary:
Fire Calendar turns twenty years of NASA fire detections into a short list a Cambodian ranger can act on.

We put MODIS (2003–2011) and VIIRS (2012–today) on one scale: we count fire-days on a 10 km grid and scale MODIS to VIIRS for each land type and season. On years the scaling was not fitted on, it cut the typical error from 74.8% to 30.5%. We wrote the rules down before touching the data. The result is a monthly fire calendar since 2003 in which the 2012 jump shows as a change of satellite, not of burning.

That record tells us what is normal for each place and week. In one January 2026 week, one satellite logged 4,524 detections in Cambodia. No patrol can check them all, and most are routine field burning. Our pre-registered rule keeps 11 places in 7 protected areas where fire was far above that place’s usual. Number one, Virachey National Park, had fire on all 7 days of a week that usually has none.

A Telegram bot sends the list in Khmer, one place at a time. People pick where to send a team first; only the team on the ground can say what the fire is.
projectDetails.details:
Fire Calendar has three parts.

1. A harmonized fire record. We downloaded NASA FIRMS hotspots for Cambodia from MODIS (2003 on) and VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20. We clean them: nominal and high confidence only, known fixed heat sources removed, inside Cambodia only, counted on local dates. We count fire as fire-days: a 10 km grid square with at least one detection on a day. MODIS is scaled to VIIRS with a factor fitted separately for each land type (ESA WorldCover) and season. We fitted it on 2012–2016 and tested it on 2017–2019. On those 470 held-out province-months, the median error against VIIRS fell from 74.8% to 30.5%. Timing agreement dipped slightly, from 0.935 to 0.924, and we report that too. The result is a monthly calendar of Cambodia’s burning from 2003 to today, in which the 2012 jump shows as a change of satellite, not of burning.

2. A look-first list. Because the record is consistent, we know what is normal for each place in each week of the year. A 10 km square is listed when four things are true: a detection falls inside a protected area, the square is mostly forest, fire was seen on at least 2 of 7 days, and that is at least double the place’s usual for the same week. For Jan 12–18, 2026, S-NPP saw 4,524 detections. That narrows to 1,490 inside protected areas, then 1,089 in forest squares, then 124 detections in 11 places across 7 protected areas. NOAA-20, run on its own, listed 10 places, and 5 of them are on both lists.

3. Delivery where rangers already are. A Telegram bot (@khmerfiresbot) sends this week’s list, or the January 2026 replay, in Khmer or English, one place at a time. Place 1 explains why it is first. Virachey National Park had fire on all 7 days; the same week had no fire in 10 of 13 earlier years. It has had 113 days with fire this year, against at most 48 in any earlier year. Each place shows its coordinates, a map link and a three-day weather line on how easily a fire could spread. People can pick where they would send a team first. The bot also sends daily alerts for a chosen pin, province or park. The web app shows the calendar, a “compared with normal” map, every detection as a point, and a monthly outlook. The outlook is clearly labelled as a model estimate.

Benefits

  • A ranger station gets about ten places to check instead of thousands of dots.
  • Each place is judged against its own past, so the unusual forest fire stands out from routine field burning.
  • It comes in Khmer, on a phone, in an app people already use, at no cost to the user.
  • The rules are public and simple enough for anyone to check.

Intended impact

We want to help the person who decides where a patrol goes each day, such as a protected-area station chief or provincial officer, send teams to the unusual fires first. This matters most in the January–March dry season. Our next step is a pilot with a ranger team from January to March. It will count how many listed places were checked, and how many the team says they would have missed. We do not claim to prevent fires; we help decide where to look.

Tools and technology

  • Pipeline: Python 3.12 with uv, pandas, GeoPandas, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, pyproj, rasterio and PyArrow. Land cover is read through Microsoft Planetary Computer.
  • Web app: TypeScript, React 19, Vite and MapLibre GL, installable and usable offline on phones.
  • Bot and hosting: Vercel serverless functions, Vercel Blob storage and a daily scheduled job, with the Telegram Bot API.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP, VIIRS NOAA-20 near-real-time), ESA WorldCover 2021, geoBoundaries, Open Development Cambodia protected areas, GBIF species records, Open-Meteo, NASA POWER and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hardware: our own laptops only.

What makes it creative

  • It treats harmonization as the means, not the end. A consistent 20-year record is what lets us say “unusual for this place, this week” rather than “a lot of fire”.
  • It ranks by surprise against a place’s own history, not by size.
  • We wrote our rules down before running them, and every later change is a dated note with its measured effect.
  • It replays a real past week as a practice mode that anyone can open with a QR code.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about the data. A hotspot is a hot pixel, not a confirmed fire. Satellites miss small, short and cloud-covered fires, so an empty list means “nothing seen”, never “safe”. We report looser versions of the rule too (34–44 places), to show how much the choice matters.
  • Safety. Every list says to keep your distance and call 118 if a fire is spreading. People cannot mark a place as fire or no fire from a phone, because someone far away could mark a real fire “nothing there”. They can only pick where to look first, and picks on the replay are kept apart as practice.
  • Language and access. Plain Khmer comes first, with the exact figures always shown.
  • Satellite changes. S-NPP stopped on Nov 2, 2026, so live weeks use NOAA-20, compared with its own past.
  • Privacy and cost. Only counts of picks are shown, never who made them. The data and Telegram are free to use, and hosting is cheap.

projectDetails.name: Project APSARALLAX
projectDetails.summary:
Martian Explorer is an interactive 2D and 3D tactical navigation web application developed for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Centered on the Amazonis Planitia–Erebus Montes region, the platform transforms raw orbital datasets into real-time traverse planning for EVA astronauts, mission planners, and autonomous rovers.

To address the challenge, we fused five NASA data streams—MOLA (elevation and slope), THEMIS (thermal inertia), HiRISE/CTX (high-resolution imagery), SWIM (water-ice probability), and DONKI (solar particle events)—into a 40,000-node multi-hazard cost grid. Powered by a custom Weighted A* pathfinding algorithm, the console calculates optimal routes in under 15 milliseconds, bending around steep ridge scarps (>15 degrees) and powdery dust traps (TIU < 95) while monitoring real-time route distance, ETA, spacesuit oxygen, and battery levels.   

Standard satellite maps show where astronauts are, but not the hidden surface hazards that threaten their survival. Martian Explorer prevents rover rollovers and crew overexertion—reducing estimated oxygen consumption by over 48%—while enabling instant emergency rerouting to natural basalt shelters during solar radiation storms and offering a lightweight, offline-ready framework adaptable for disaster response on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
MARTIAN EXPLORER — INTERPLANETARY SURVIVAL GUIDE: MARTIAN MAP

Martian Explorer is an interactive, 100% client-side 2D and 3D tactical navigation web console built by Team APSARALLAX. Focused on the Amazonis Planitia – Erebus Montes sector (39.89°N–40.05°N, 190.75°E–191.00°E), it transforms five raw NASA orbital datasets into real-time, hazard-aware traverse planning for EVA astronauts, mission planners, and autonomous rovers.

1. WHAT DOES IT DO & HOW DOES IT WORK?

On Mars, satellite imagery alone is deceptive—a flat-looking plain on an optical map can hide wheel-trapping dust mantles, steep scarps, and unshielded radiation zones. Martian Explorer solves this by combining multi-spectral orbital data fusion with a real-time pathfinding engine that runs entirely inside the browser with zero backend server dependencies:

• Multi-Layer Opacity Blender: Users can toggle and blend five co-registered NASA data layers—HiRISE/CTX (5m optical base imagery), MOLA (digital elevation model and derived slope hazards), THEMIS (nighttime infrared thermal inertia), SWIM (subsurface water-ice probability), and DONKI (solar particle event radiation modeling).

• Offline-First Multi-Hazard Cost Grid: Because Mars surface missions face a 4-to-24-minute communication delay and have no live cloud internet, we designed an offline preprocessing pipeline (Reproject → Resample → Tile → Normalize). It compresses gigabytes of raw NASA GeoTIFFs into a <5 MB static bundle containing a uniform 200 × 200 computational grid (40,000 nodes at 200 m/cell) stored in contiguous JavaScript TypedArrays (Float32Array / Uint8Array).

• Weighted A* Pathfinding Engine (<15 ms): When a user selects a scientific point of interest (AP-1 through AP-9), our in-browser 8-connected Weighted A* solver evaluates all 40,000 nodes in under 15 milliseconds using the step-cost function:

Δg(n) = d_step × (1 + w_slope · R_slope(n) + w_dust · R_dust(n) + w_rad · R_rad(n))

- Hard No-Go Zones: Slopes > 15° are blocked as impassable rollover hazards, slopes between 7°–15° receive caution penalties, and slopes < 7° are prioritized as safe corridors.

- Dust Trap Avoidance: Regions with low thermal inertia (TIU < 95) are penalized to prevent rovers and astronauts from sinking into loose, powdery regolith.

• Mission Planner & Life-Support Telemetry: Supporting both Rover and Foot (EVA) modes, the console integrates distance, slope grade, and surface drag along the route to calculate real-time Route Distance, ETA, Suit Oxygen (O₂) Used, and Battery Remaining (for example, validating a safe 27.49 km rover traverse to debris-apron target AP-1 in 4h 57m using 21% O₂ and 73% Battery). If a route exceeds safe life-support margins, the console automatically flags a CREW SAFETY CAUTION or CREW SAFETY NO-GO alert.

• Solar Storm (SPE) Emergency Rerouting: Clicking SIMULATE SOLAR STORM (SPE) overrides active science objectives when radiation spikes (modeling surges up to 1,450 mSv/hr) and instantly computes the fastest evacuation vector to the nearest natural basalt ridge or alcove shelter (S-1 through S-16).

• Synchronized 2D Tactical Map & 3D Terrain Orbit: Planners can switch seamlessly between the 2D tactical map and an interactive 3D WebGL terrain mesh displaced by MOLA elevation data to inspect ridge shadows and scarp geometry from any angle.

2. BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT

• Astronaut & Rover Survival: Replaces risky straight-line navigation with hazard-aware paths, preventing catastrophic rover rollovers on >15° scarps and wheel entrapment in soft dust.

• 48%+ Oxygen & Energy Conservation: Benchmarking across our 40,000-node Erebus Montes grid shows that routing around steep inclines and high-drag dust reduces cumulative traversal exertion and estimated spacesuit oxygen consumption by over 48%.

• Decision Support for Mission Planners: Eliminates the bottleneck of manually cross-referencing separate orbital maps, turning hours of route validation and emergency contingency planning into a sub-15 ms workflow.

• Applications on Earth: Because the engine runs 100% offline in a standard browser without a backend server, the exact same multi-layer cost-grid architecture can guide disaster-relief teams on Earth after floods, earthquakes, or landslides destroy road networks and cellular connectivity.

3. TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE & SOFTWARE USED

• Architecture: 100% Client-Side Single-Page Application (Serverless / No Backend). All pathfinding, telemetry calculation, and 3D rendering execute locally in the browser (~770 MB active RAM footprint).

• Frontend & Rendering: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 2D Canvas API (multi-layer raster compositing), and WebGL / Three.js (3D DEM terrain mesh displacement and dynamic texture draping).

• Algorithms & Data Structures: Custom Weighted A* pathfinder built on flat 1D Float32Array / Uint8Array memory buffers and a binary min-heap priority queue for zero-latency execution.

• Geospatial Preprocessing: Python (GDAL, Rasterio, NumPy) for offline coordinate reprojection, 200 m/cell resampling, 3×3 Sobel slope-gradient derivation, and [0, 1] hazard normalization.

• NASA Datasets & Sources:

- MOLA (DEM): USGS Astrogeology PDS & NASA Mars Trek (Elevation & slope risk)

- THEMIS: ASU Mars Space Flight Facility / PDS Geosciences Node (Nighttime IR thermal inertia)

- HiRISE / CTX: NASA PDS Imaging Node & Caltech Murray Lab (High-resolution optical imagery)

- SWIM / SHARAD: NASA Subsurface Water Ice Mapping Project (Water-ice probability for ISRU/science sites)

- DONKI: NASA CCMC Space Weather Database (Solar Particle Event radiation modeling)

• Hardware: Developed and benchmarked on an ASUS ROG Strix workstation (NVIDIA RTX 4080 GPU) and tested across standard desktop and tablet browsers.

4. HOW IS OUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

• Using Nighttime Heat to Detect Invisible Dust Traps: Optical satellite cameras cannot tell the difference between solid bedrock and deep, powdery dust if they share the same color. We creatively integrated THEMIS nighttime thermal inertia (TIU < 95)—which measures how quickly surface material loses heat after sunset—directly into our A* mechanical drag cost function.

• Natural Topography as Emergency Radiation Shelters: Mars lacks a global magnetic field. Instead of assuming astronauts can always return to their main habitat during a sudden Solar Particle Event, we used MOLA elevation gradients to index 16 natural basalt ridge scarps and alcoves (S-1 to S-16) that provide immediate horizon shielding against incoming solar protons.

• True Mars-Ready Serverless Engineering: Rather than building a cloud backend that would be unusable on Mars due to deep-space communication blackouts, we engineered our entire geospatial stack to run locally inside a static browser bundle in <15 ms.

5. KEY FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

• Spatial Resolution vs. Compute Speed: We balanced visual fidelity against real-time responsiveness by pairing a sharp 5m/pixel CTX/HiRISE visual base map with a 200m/cell computational hazard grid. We also transparently documented our system's operational boundaries: while a 200m grid captures regional slopes and dust basins, detecting sub-meter boulders requires local rover LiDAR integration (planned in our Future Roadmap alongside expanding to Jezero Crater, Arcadia Planitia, and multi-agent rover/astronaut coordination).

• Real-World EVA Physiology & Hardware Limits: Every route is evaluated against realistic spacesuit oxygen and rover battery budgets so mission planners never approve a path that strands a crew outside their safe return radius.

• High-Stress Tactical UX: We used a clean blue, dark-navy, and high-contrast white/mint tactical palette with unmistakable GO / CAUTION / NO-GO telemetry badges so astronauts and planners can read critical hazard alerts at a glance.

projectDetails.name: Earth Buddy
projectDetails.summary: Earth Buddy is tackling the trend detective challenge, which solves the problem of stakeholders such as farmers and civilians being impacted by events such as the El Niño drought. The data fails to fully acknowledge to the stakeholders the potential harm future change may do. Earth Buddy simplifies mathematical models and complex data visualization to an agentic SI where key stakeholders and key players could retrieve tested trends and warn the impacted groups of people. The trends are done through a pipeline in Python through multimathematical models such as the Mann-Kendall significance, Sen's slope, STL decomposition, memory correction, Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate, and Pettitt change point test and t-tests to cross-check between the results. In this pilot-testing stage, heat, rain, soil moisture, humidity, evaporation, water vapor, the ozone layer, and other key variables are used for us to find the trends and test their significance. With the technology of the hosted Telegram bot with text-to-speech and speech-to-text both in Khmer and in English, this could lower the technological barrier to understanding this trend and get prepare for any potential impact the events may have on the community, province, sector, country, and region.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Earth Buddy is an Earth system trend detective for Cambodia, Southeast Asia, and the world. Anyone can ask a plain question in Khmer or English via the Telegram bot or the website, such as "Is Phnom Penh getting hotter?" or "Cambodia is getting hotter and drier," and Earth Buddy answers from NASA data with a tested verdict, not a guess.

It works in four steps through an agentic chatbot interface:

1. Ask: a reader turns the sentence into a structured question (a claim to check, a trend, a scan of every measure for a place, or a map of where change is strongest).

2. Data: Earth Buddy loads 24 years of NASA data (2001–2024) for that place: 27 variables from MERRA-2, CERES, GPM IMERG, and MODIS active fires, served through NASA POWER and FIRMS, with any map point fetched live and cached.

3. Analyze: a statistics engine decides every verdict. Sen's slope measures the size of the change. The Mann-Kendall test checks whether it is real, corrected for climate's year-to-year memory so a run of hot or wet years is not mistaken for a trend. A Pettitt change-point test separates a sudden jump from a steady trend, and a Benjamini-Hochberg check controls false discoveries when many variables are tested at once.

4. Explain: the result is written in plain Khmer or English for a student, a policymaker, or the general public with some scientific backgrounds. The AI only writes words from the computed result; any text containing a number that is not in the result is rejected and replaced by a template. With the SI switched off, every verdict is identical. The purpose of the SI is to eliminate the technical and communication barriers between the user and the output.

Example: for Phnom Penh, Earth Buddy finds warming of about 0.37°C per decade, but after correcting for year-to-year memory, the evidence is not strong enough to rule out chance (p = 0.29). It says so honestly: "not proven yet," not "no change." For Tonle Sap, NASA GRACE water storage shows a clear fall of about 7.6 cm per decade since 2002 (p = 0.019), an early signal for the fishing and farming families around the lake.

BENEFITS

- Trustworthy: every number comes from NASA data and a fixed, tested statistics engine. We measured the engine on thousands of simulated series: on trend-free data it raises a false alarm 3–6% of the time, close to the 5% it promises, whereas the uncorrected test reaches 14–22%. This balances between the power and the false positive so that the results can be trusted and acted on.

- Honest about uncertainty: every answer shows the size of the change, a 95% range, and a plain-language level (clear, likely, or unclear), so nobody has to read a p-value to understand it.

- Accessible: Khmer and English, three reading levels, no account needed, and a Telegram bot pilot so answers reach people on the app they already use.

- Transparent: each answer lists its NASA sources, the method steps, and the years tested.

INTENDED IMPACT

Cambodia's forecasts and early warnings "are not readily accessible to everyone and often not updated regularly" (World Bank, Cambodia Country Climate and Development Report, 2023). The same report estimates Cambodia could avoid up to US$340 million a year in well-being losses with universal early warning. After the 2015–16 El Niño drought, a WFP, UNICEF, FAO, and NCDM survey of 2,400 households in 160 villages found paddy and cassava output down 22%, 62% of households losing income, 37% short of water, and an average of USD 1,282 in new debt.

Earth Buddy aims to close that gap: to let farmers, teachers, journalists, local planners, and agencies check climate claims against NASA data before they repeat them and to turn real, tested trends into early, plain-language signals. Our next step is a Telegram pilot in one drought-prone province (Prey Veng or Kampong Speu), working toward partners such as NCDM, MAFF, MOWRAM, and humanitarian agencies.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: Python (back end and statistics), JavaScript, HTML, and CSS (web app).

- Back end: FastAPI and Uvicorn, Pydantic, httpx, and SQLite cache.

- Statistics: NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, statsmodels (STL seasonal decomposition).

- Front end: MapLibre GL for maps, custom charts, and Khmer and English interfaces.

- AI: Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock for plain-language text only, behind a number check, with templates as a fallback.

- NASA data: MERRA-2 (via NASA POWER), CERES SYN1deg, GPM IMERG, MODIS active fires (FIRMS), GRACE total water storage.

- Testing and deployment: 164 automated pytest tests, including a test that verifies the verdict is unchanged with the AI off and a test that only NASA sources are used; deployed on Vercel. Telegram bot pilot at t.me/EarthBuddyBot.

- Hardware: standard laptops and cloud services; no special hardware.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It treats climate claims like a detective case: the user brings a claim, and Earth Buddy brings the NASA evidence and a verdict.

- It separates language from computation. The AI never makes a number, so a fluent answer can never be a made-up one.

- It is honest about what 24 years of data can show. "Unclear" is a real answer, explained as "can't tell yet," which most climate tools never say.

- It tells a sudden jump apart from a steady trend and corrects for climate's memory, so it does not cry wolf.

- It brings research-grade statistics to Khmer speakers in their language and on the messaging app they already use.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Trust: only NASA data, every source cited, every verdict reproducible, and a test that proves the AI cannot change a result.

- Statistical honesty: year-to-year memory, many tests at once, sudden jumps versus trends, and the limits of a 24-year record. We simulated our own error rates rather than assume them.

- Language and audience: Khmer first, plain words, and different detail for students, policymakers, and the general public with some scientific background.

- Reach: low-bandwidth delivery through Telegram rather than another app to install; village chiefs can forward a message to a whole community.

- Limits we state openly: the roughly 55 km satellite grid smooths over village micro-climates; we track environmental risk, not health outcomes; short records often cannot prove small trends; and Telegram channel delivery is still a pilot.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT: Terratoria
projectDetails.summary: On humanity's journey back to the Moon, sustained human operations and settlements is a question to be answered. Regarding this, our team utilized NASA data to search for and analog locations on Earth to Mars and the Moon, where certain matching standards (i.e. terrain, biosphere, geology, temperature etc...) can be used to test and further hone plans for establishment. This is a stepping stone towards a greater benchmark in deep-space exploration and scientific discovery, as well as the potential for long-term survival.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

PROJECT: Terratoria is a web tool that finds and explains places on Earth that are most like future landing and base sites on the Moon and Mars. It compares 21 Earth sites (18 known analogue sites and 3 untested candidates we propose) with four reference regions: Shackleton crater and the Marius Hills pit on the Moon, and Jezero crater and Arsia Mons on Mars.

Each Earth site is scored against each region across the eight dimensions in the challenge: terrain; geology and materials; temperature and light; water and ice; dust and wind; biology and habitability; caves and subsurface; and exploration operations.

- Measured from open data: terrain, temperature and wind.
- Terrain comes from NASA LRO LOLA (Moon), NASA MGS MOLA (Mars) and ESA Copernicus DEM (Earth). We process a 60 km window around every site, at the same scale for every world, into slope, relief, roughness and elevation profiles.
- Temperature comes from NASA LRO Diviner (Moon), NASA POWER (Earth) and Perseverance MEDA results (Mars).
- From the literature: the other dimensions come from peer-reviewed studies and the USGS list of known terrestrial analogue sites. Every characteristic is linked to its source in APA style.

The scores combine into an Exploratory Analogue Similarity Index. Users can change how much each dimension matters. Missing data lowers the "coverage" figure, never the score, so a site is never punished for being under-studied. Every result shows its evidence, its data source, and where Earth falls short.

Main features
- Discover: a ranked map of all sites.
- 3D Explorer: rotating 3D Earth, Moon and Mars with clickable sites.
- Site pages: 2D and 3D terrain views, charts and real photographs.
- Compare: up to three sites side by side.
- Mission Plan: five steps toward a lunar base, each matched to the Earth sites where it can be tested first.
- Mission Challenge: four learning games (Quiz, Rush, Flashcards and Touchdown, a rocket-landing game where only gravity changes between worlds).
- Saved sites, CSV export and printable reports.

Benefits and intended impact

Analogue sites are where mission teams test rovers, drills, habitats and crews before they fly, but the challenge notes that many of these sites are not well characterised. Terratoria puts the evidence for each site in one place, measured the same way across all three worlds, so a researcher or mission planner can quickly see which site suits which test, and why.

We also built it for students. It works in English and Khmer and has a Simple mode, so learners in Cambodia and elsewhere can explore real planetary data in their own language. The games teach how to read terrain and temperature data instead of just presenting facts.

We were honest about limits throughout. Terratoria is a screening tool, not a scientific classification. All data are archived products, not live observations, and the site states its known weaknesses openly.

Tools, languages and software
- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
- Framework: Next.js 16 with React 19, exported as a static website so it cannot go down during judging.
- Visuals: Three.js for 3D globes, terrain and space scenes; MapLibre GL for the map; Recharts for charts.
- Styling and motion: Tailwind CSS, GSAP and Lenis.
- Data processing: Node.js scripts using geotiff, run once to turn raw NASA and ESA data into small JSON files.
- Testing: Vitest, with 62 unit tests and 6 pipeline tests. They check the scoring maths, that every citation exists, and that every image is credited.
- Sound: the Web Audio API.
- Promo video: HyperFrames.
- Hosting: GitHub and GitHub Pages.
- AI: the code was written with AI assistance (Claude) from our own concept, research and design decisions.
- Hardware: only our laptops; no special hardware was needed.

How it is creative

Instead of a plain table of scores, Terratoria lets you fly between worlds: a 3D solar system on the home page, globes you can spin, and terrain you can view in 3D at the same scale on Earth, the Moon and Mars. Learning is turned into play through quizzes, flashcards and a rocket-landing game, all built from the same data as the rankings. We also added a dark space design, a custom cursor made from our team logo, and optional theme songs.

Factors our team considered
- Scientific honesty: measured data and literature-based data are labelled separately, every claim is cited, and missing data is never hidden.
- Fair comparison: the same window size and pixel scale on every world, and no image stretched or recoloured to look more similar.
-Accessibility:
- Colour palettes for every type of colour blindness.
- Lite Mode for older phones and laptops with little memory.
- Reduced-motion support.
- Keyboard controls.
- Khmer translation.
- Copyright: we used only openly licensed data and images, credited every photo, font, library and song, and marked fan-tribute themes as unofficial.
- Reliability: a static site with no server or login, so judges can always open it.

projectDetails.name: Project Astropeers
projectDetails.summary:
Outpost Darkside is a free browser game for children aged 7–12 where players manage a small base on the far side of the Moon. They must build essential systems, including solar panels, oxygen production, a greenhouse, and radiation protection, to keep an astronaut alive until sunrise.
Each mission is based on a real week of space weather from NASA's DONKI database, ranging from calm solar conditions in 2019 to the massive Gannon storm in May 2024. Players must respond to solar storms while managing limited resources. Every decision has consequences, whether it's saving battery power for the two-week lunar night or building faster to make progress.
To complete the mission, players also drive a rover to photograph five real craters using NASA and Artemis II images.
Through gameplay, children learn how solar activity affects space exploration, why astronauts need life-support systems, and how to make decisions when resources are limited. By working with real NASA data, they gain a practical understanding of the science and problem-solving involved in living on the Moon, skills that future explorers will need.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does and how it works: The player picks one of four missions, each a real week of solar activity and together a difficulty ladder: Calm Sun, Busy Sun, This Month and Solar Storm. Four picture cards explain the game, and a one-tap starter pack fills the ship.



    On the Moon the player walks to flags to build, while a checklist and a "do this now" line show the next job. Each day the player picks one of two or three choices, and small bars preview how each choice changes power, oxygen, air, water, food and radiation dose against its limit. The last days of every mission are the lunar night, with no solar power. Real solar events from NASA's records appear as alerts, and every option has a visible cost.

    Once the rover is built, the player can spend a day photographing craters, and the real NASA photo is revealed afterwards. A debrief shows each day's choice next to the best one, explains cause and effect, and gives a real science fact from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.
  • Benefits: The game teaches systems thinking (every choice saves one thing and costs another), real space science and how to read data, all through play. It works on desktop, tablet and phone, needs no install or account, and can be explained in a 30-second demo, so it suits classrooms and science fairs.
  • Intended impact: We want children to understand that living on the Moon is a puzzle of power, air, water, food and safety, that the Sun's weather is real and measurable, and that scientists use data like NASA's to make decisions. We hope it sparks an interest in space science and STEM careers, especially in children who would not pick up a textbook.
  • Tools, languages, hardware and software: JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas and the Phaser 4 game engine; Vite for building; Vitest for automated tests; the Web Audio API for all sound, generated in code; Node.js scripts that cache NASA data from the DONKI, NASA Image and Video Library and OSDR APIs; Playwright scripts for automated play-tests; and Git and GitHub. An AI coding assistant (Claude) also helped documentation, write and test code. The game runs in any modern browser, so no special hardware is needed.

  • Creativity: We turned space weather from a chart into a place you have to survive. Each mission is a real calendar week, so the player lives through the May 2024 storm day by day, and a quiet week in 2019 really does feel calm. When the lunar night falls, a child feels why a battery matters before reading a word about it. Every choice is a small dilemma with a price, and the best call changes with the situation, so there is no answer to memorise. Failure is gentle: the crew is sent home to the ISS, and the debrief shows what to change next time. The rover turns waiting into adventure, revealing a real NASA crater photo, including Artemis II images, like a postcard from an actual Moon mission.
  • Factors we considered:
    (1) Audience: children aged 7 to 12, so plain text of about 12 words or fewer per message, with icons instead of paragraphs.
    (2) Intuitive play: icons, a checklist, a "do this now" line and a one-tap starter pack let players learn by doing, without reading instructions.
    (3) Fun and focus: we balanced learning with fun, kept the main objective in front of the player (build the base and reach sunrise), and cut anything that did not serve it.
    (4) Honesty: real data is labelled with its source and date and never called "live", and simplified numbers are labelled as simplified.
    (5) Accessibility: large touch targets, keyboard, mouse and touch controls, no hover-only information, and sound that can be turned off.
    (6) Privacy: NASA data is cached at build time, the game makes no network calls while playing, and it collects no personal data.
    (7) Fairness: automated tests check that every mission can be won and that no choice is free.
    (8) Copyright: glossary definitions are our own and credit NASA Space Place, and every photo carries its NASA credit.

projectDetails.name: Astro-SI: an on-board health copilot for a Mars crew
projectDetails.summary: On the way to Mars, nobody flies home, and a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way. Astro-SI is an on-board health copilot that lets the crew check and act on their own health. It follows 4 crew members minute by minute over a 180-day transit, learns each person's normal in the first two weeks, and warns early on all 5 NASA Human Research Program hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and the hostile closed environment. Every alert ends in numbered steps the crew can do on board now, plus the questions to send to Earth and when the reply will arrive. It also warns of solar radiation storms from onboard sensors, guides a medical emergency step by step, and answers questions through "Astro", a voice and text chat that cites its sources and never decides an alert. The data is simulated but built on real measurements: ISS radiation, real solar storms, Inspiration4 blood tests and real wearable recordings. The engine scores itself: on 12 unseen test missions it caught 93.3% of health events at 0.294 false alarms per crew-month, against 49.8% for fixed limits.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Astro-SI is a mission console for a 4-person crew on a 180-day Mars transit. It replays per-minute signals (heart rate, sleep, activity, blood pressure, HRV, blood oxygen, breathing, skin temperature, blood sugar, radiation dose, solar X-ray, proton and electron flux, cabin CO2 and noise) plus a daily mood, fatigue and reaction-time check.

  • Your normal, not an average. Days 1-14 learn each crew member's own baseline. A random forest and an isolation forest, trained in Rust, score drift from that personal normal. Fixed safety limits (dose, CO2, blood oxygen, noise) still fire on their own.
  • All 5 NASA HRP hazards. Each alert names its hazard and NASA risk, shows which signals made it fire, and says whether the crew can treat it on board.
  • Built for the radio delay. Every alert splits into "Do now on board" (numbered steps with tick boxes) and "Ask Earth" (with the reply time from the live Earth-Mars distance, and "Don't wait: act now" when the reply would come too late). One click drafts a short report for Earth.
  • Radiation storm warning. "Storm likely within 6 h: go to shelter", from onboard X-ray and proton sensors, trained on real NOAA GOES data 2010-2026 and tested on years the model never saw.
  • Emergency guide. A red Emergency button opens step-by-step help for a collapsed or unwell crewmate (CPR in microgravity, current readings against their normal, a prefilled message to Earth). Fixed, sourced steps; never written by the AI.
  • Astro, the crew chat. Ask by text or say "Hey Astro". Answers come only from a fixed pack of NASA rules and verified facts, with cited sources. It understands everyday words ("dizzy when I stand up"), never diagnoses or gives doses, marks any number it cannot find in its sources, and offers "Send to Earth" when it does not know.
  • The six challenge indicators. Blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood, each against the person's own normal, with a daily routine to tick off. The crew can also type their own readings.
  • 3D body view. A figure that lights up the body system that needs attention.
  • Medicine cabinet. Which medicines run out or expire before the crew gets home.
  • Space / Earth switch. The same alerts switch to Earth-side advice, for remote clinics, polar stations or home care.

How it is built

  • Data pipeline (Python): real NASA and NOAA data plus real wearable recordings become a seeded, per-minute 180-day mission.
  • Engine (Rust compiled to WebAssembly): baselines, machine learning, rules, storm warning, forecast and self-scoring, all in the browser. 1.55 million crew-minute readings per second natively; the browser runs days 1-91 in 574 ms.
  • Console (React, TypeScript, Vite), with the engine in a background worker.
  • AI: DeepSeek stands in for the onboard AI (its model weights are public, so the same model could run on the ship); a local model (LM Studio, Ollama) works by changing one address. The AI only rewords alerts the rules decided and answers questions. It never raises, changes or clears an alert. If it is down, built-in text is shown.

Tools

Rust, WebAssembly, TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js, Python (numpy, pandas, scipy), Node.js, headless Chrome for tests, DeepSeek API. Runs on any laptop or phone with a modern browser.

What we considered

  • Accessibility: plain-language alerts for a crew that are not doctors, colour plus text for every severity, keyboard shortcuts, phone and tablet layouts, reduced-motion support.
  • Cost and power: free open tools, public data, one small engine that runs offline in the browser.
  • Safety: rules decide every alert; the AI key never reaches the browser.

Results (on our own labelled synthetic missions, not clinical accuracy)

  • 12 unseen test missions, 480 events: 93.3% caught, 0.294 false alarms per crew-month; fixed limits caught 49.8%.
  • Showcase: Day 90 real May 2024 solar storm caught after 0.82 h; Day 135 sleep deficit caught after 32.7 h, which fixed limits missed.
  • Storm warning on real 2022-2025 storms: 34 of 36 caught, median 1.46 h notice; the May 2024 storm warned 6.0 h ahead.
  • AI exam, 132 team-written questions: grounded chat 130 of 132, the same AI without our sources 106 of 132.

Honest limits

Heart rate, sleep, activity and mood are real recordings from healthy volunteers, not astronauts; the other vitals and cabin sensors are simulated and labelled so. Health events are planted so the engine can score itself. ISS radiation is lower than deep space. A simple tuned rule matches our storm model. No doctor graded the alerts or the exam. Full methods: the research paper in the repo.

Use of SI (AI tools)

  • In the product: DeepSeek stands in for the onboard AI. It rewords alerts the rules already decided and answers crew questions from a fixed set of sources it cites. It never raises, changes or clears an alert.
  • Code and data: the team used AI coding assistants to help write, test and review code, and to help analyse results. The team checked the output, and every number we quote comes from a test run in our repository.
  • Research and writing: AI tools helped find sources and draft text. Each fact in the chat's knowledge pack was checked against a quote saved from its original source.
  • Audio: the demo video's voice-over is AI-generated (ElevenLabs) and is labelled "AI-generated voice" on screen.
  • Images and video: the video shows real screen recordings of our app, not AI-generated footage. No NASA logos, flags or mission patches appear in any AI-made content.
  • Logo: the Astro-SI logo is AI-generated and is marked "AI-generated logo" where it appears.

projectDetails.name: Project Big Boss
projectDetails.summary: We want to build an interactive game-like app that can simplify complex NASA data into an engaging and accessible app. When it comes to accessibility there is a wide range we would like to address the language barriers. By integrating an automatic translating system where the players can select their language and the game will translate to that automatically. Many people including us find scientific data to be super duper interesting and fascinating but too hard to grasp to even be remembered for future flexing. So our app aims to fill this gap by turning the learning process about the universe into a fun game rather than a traditional learning method (who even likes reading books).
projectDetails.details:
Our Project Solution

Our project is an interactive educational adventure game designed to make complex NASA scientific data fun, understandable, and accessible to everyone. Through a futuristic, story-driven experience, players become astronauts travelling back in time to 2026 to prevent Earth's destruction caused by climate change and pollution. By turning real environmental challenges into interactive missions, we aim to make learning about our planet an adventure rather than a traditional classroom experience.

How Does Our Solution Work?

In the game, players take on the role of an astronaut who failed to find a habitable planet before Earth was destroyed. Given a second chance to return to 2026, they must travel across different continents, investigate environmental challenges such as air pollution, global warming, and rising sea levels, and discover possible solutions. Each continent features missions powered by real NASA data, allowing players to interact with datasets like FIRMS active fire data to track wildfires, GEOS aerosols to visualize air quality, and GEDI forest height data to restore deforested regions. By exploring these environmental changes, understanding their impacts, and completing quests, players unlock new regions. With built-in automatic translation and audio accessibility features, players can learn in their preferred language, making scientific knowledge more inclusive and engaging.

How did we code?
To develop the project, we utilized Visual Studio Code as the primary code editor and development environment. The application was built using foundational web technologies, specifically HTML to structure the semantic layout, CSS for styling and responsive interface design, and JavaScript to manage client-side interactivity and dynamic functionality. Additionally, AI tools were leveraged to assist with multi-language implementation and to integrate the Google Gemini API, enabling intelligent processing and interactive features within the application.

Who Benefits From Our Solution?

Our game benefits students, educators, and the wider community by:

  • Making science accessible: By simplifying complex NASA data and environmental information so everyone can understand it, regardless of their language or scientific background we're able to make learning more accessible to people.
  • Raising environmental awareness: Helping players recognize real-world environmental challenges, including air pollution, climate change, and rising sea levels, and understand their impacts on our planet.
  • Encouraging critical thinking: Challenging players to investigate environmental problems, explore possible solutions, and think about how they can contribute to protecting Earth.
  • Making learning engaging: Turning scientific education into an interactive adventure that encourages curiosity, exploration, and long-term knowledge retention.
  • Bridging the information gap: Connecting NASA's scientific discoveries and datasets with everyday people through simplified explanations, visualizations, and multilingual accessibility.

projectDetails.name: BurnScan: Harmonized MODIS & VIIRS Fire Monitoring Dashboard
projectDetails.summary: BurnScan is an interactive web dashboard that unifies 25+ years of incompatible NASA satellite fire detections—MODIS (2000–present, 1 km resolution) and VIIRS (2012–present, 375 m resolution)—into a single, calibrated historical and regional monitoring baseline. Because VIIRS detects much smaller fires and uses categorical confidence levels (low, nominal, high) while MODIS uses a 0–100 scale, combining raw counts creates an artificial spike in 2012 that misleads responders. BurnScan harmonizes sensor confidence scores, normalizes detections across a unified spatial grid, and visualizes burning patterns across Cambodia’s 24 provinces and Phnom Penh. Built for provincial environment officers, disaster-management teams, and researchers, BurnScan replaces fragmented archives with clear seasonal calendars, intensity maps, and filterable records so communities can distinguish real climate-driven fire anomalies from sensor artifacts.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem We Solve

Satellites have tracked global active fires for over two decades, yet the historical record is fractured across two incompatible NASA sensors: MODIS (operational since 2000 at 1 km pixel resolution, reporting confidence from 0–100) and VIIRS (operational since 2012 at 375 m resolution, reporting categorical confidence as low, nominal, or high). Because VIIRS resolves fires roughly 7× smaller by pixel area and captures different overpass dynamics, plotting raw combined counts creates an artificial jump in 2012. In our own live NASA FIRMS data pull (October 25, 2026), an 8-day global window yielded 81,177 MODIS detections versus 477,946 VIIRS detections. Without harmonization, emergency responders, agricultural officers, and researchers cannot separate genuine burning trends from sensor-upgrade artifacts.

How BurnScan Does & Key Features BurnScan transforms multi-decade MODIS and VIIRS fire records into an interactive, decision-ready monitoring platform tailored for regional analysis (featuring full administrative filtering across Cambodia’s 24 provinces and Phnom Penh):

  • Interactive Geospatial Hotspot Map (Leaflet.js): Plots active fire detections color-coded by Fire Radiative Power (FRP in MW) and confidence tiers, with map/satellite base-layer switching, custom zoom/layer controls, and clickable detection popups displaying timestamp, sensor, coordinates, FRP, and harmonized confidence.
  • Cross-Sensor Confidence & Grid Harmonization: Maps MODIS numerical confidence (0–29 Low, 30–79 Nominal, 80–100 High) and VIIRS categorical flags (l, n, h) onto a unified 1 / 2 / 3 confidence rank and standardized spatial grid (grid_id), enabling apples-to-apples multi-year comparisons without the 2012 sensor bias.
  • Burning Activity Calendar: A visual calendar heatmap displaying daily and weekly fire activity across the year, allowing users to spot peak smoke/burning seasons at a glance and inspect underlying detections.
  • Historical Analytics & Data Explorer: Interactive charts and searchable, exportable data tables supporting filtering by date range, province/city, sensor, confidence rank, and fire radiative power (frp_mw), alongside CSV/Parquet-compatible schema mapping.
  • Responsive Multi-Device UI: Built with light/dark mode toggling, sticky navigation, and a mobile-responsive layout (top-right filter drawer and bottom navigation bar) for field and desktop use.
  • Sensor Comparison Mode & Early-Warning Outlook: Allows toggling between MODIS-only, VIIRS-only, and Harmonized views to visualize how calibration removes the 2012 jump, paired with weekly anomaly classification (Normal, Unusual, Critical) to support proactive smoke-season readiness.

How It Works (Data Pipeline)

  1. Ingestion: Extracts MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active fire records from NASA FIRMS (sensor, satellite, date, timestamp_utc, latitude, longitude, brightness_primary, brightness_secondary, frp_mw, confidence).
  2. Standardization & Spatial Join: Harmonizes confidence metrics into unified ranks (1–3), assigns detections to a consistent spatial grid (grid_id), and enriches records with administrative province boundaries.
  3. Frontend Visualization: Serves processed datasets into a modular, lightweight web client for instant client-side filtering, mapping, and tabular export.

Impact & Future Vision BurnScan empowers provincial environmental agencies, agricultural extension officers, and disaster-management planners to identify critical burning weeks early, issue timely public health alerts before severe smoke events, and evaluate long-term climate anomalies using one continuous baseline. Next steps include automating live daily FIRMS API ingestion, integrating burned-area and land-cover layers (cropland vs. forest), and expanding administrative boundaries across Southeast Asia.

Tools, Languages & Hardware Used

  • Data Processing & Analysis: Python (Pandas, GeoPandas, PyArrow/Parquet, Folium).
  • Frontend Web Application: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, modular Vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet.js (interactive mapping), Chart.js / data tables, deployed via Vercel.
  • Collaboration & Version Control: GitHub, VS Code (Live Server).

projectDetails.name: Journey to Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Journey to Moon and Mars is an interactive educational website that allows users to explore space exploration technology through 3D visualization, animations, and storytelling. Our project focuses on two remarkable machines: the Apollo Lunar Module, which helped astronauts reach the Moon's surface, and NASA's Perseverance Rover, which explores the Martian environment.

Through interactive 3D models, component exploration, mechanical animations, and audio storytelling, users can discover how these machines work, understand their important components, and learn about their contributions to space exploration.

Our project addresses the challenge by making space technology more engaging and accessible, especially for young learners. We aim to show that every piece of space exploration equipment has a story worth understanding and remembering, even beyond its original mission.
projectDetails.details:
1. What the Project Does

Journey to Moon and Mars is an interactive educational website designed to help people explore space exploration equipment through 3D visualization and storytelling.

The project focuses on two remarkable pieces of space technology: the Apollo Lunar Module and NASA's Perseverance Mars Rover.

Users can visit dedicated Moon and Mars pages to explore 3D models, rotate and inspect the equipment, discover individual components, and learn about their functions. The website also includes mechanical animations and audio storytelling to make the learning experience more interactive.

2. Benefits and Intended Impact

Space technology can be complicated, especially for people who are unfamiliar with spacecraft engineering. Traditional educational materials often rely heavily on text and static images.

Our project aims to make learning about space technology more accessible and engaging through interactive visual experiences.

It is particularly intended for students and young space enthusiasts who want to understand how space exploration equipment works. By exploring these machines, users can develop a greater appreciation for engineering, scientific innovation, and humanity's achievements in space exploration.

3. Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5 – Building the website structure.
  • CSS3 – Designing the visual layout and appearance.
  • JavaScript – Implementing interactions and functionality.
  • Three.js – Rendering and displaying interactive 3D models.
  • GLTFLoader – Loading 3D equipment models.
  • Vite – Development environment and production build tool.
  • Netlify – Hosting and publishing the website.

4. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of this project is combining interactive 3D technology with educational storytelling.

Instead of simply presenting information about space equipment, users can interact with the machines themselves. They can rotate the models, explore selected components, observe mechanical animations, and listen to narrated explanations.

This approach transforms learning from simply reading information into an experience where users can visually explore and understand space technology.

5. Development Considerations

During development, we considered several factors:

  • Making complex engineering concepts easier to understand.
  • Creating an intuitive interface for beginners.
  • Providing interactive visual experiences rather than relying only on text.
  • Ensuring that 3D models and animations work within a web browser.
  • Organizing information into separate Moon and Mars exploration experiences.
  • Acknowledging the original sources of external 3D models and resources.

Through this project, we hope to encourage curiosity about space exploration and remind people that the machines behind these missions have important stories worth discovering and remembering.

projectDetails.name: SARWATCH - Cambodia Flood and Agriculture Explorer
projectDetails.summary: SARWATCH is an interactive Earth-observation prototype that helps people explore flooding and agriculture in Cambodia’s Tonlé Sap region. We combine team-processed outputs reported as NISAR data with rainfall and vegetation information in an accessible website. The Flood Explorer compares 11 dated water layers and displays team-reported population, road and cropland overlap estimates. The Agriculture Explorer shows cropland radar-change signals across six provinces, alongside rainfall and historical vegetation charts. Users can compare dates, select provinces and inspect sources and limitations. Designed for local planners, NGOs, agricultural advisers, researchers and students, SARWATCH addresses Dancing with the SARs by making complex radar information easier to investigate and communicate. Results remain exploratory and unreviewed, supporting further investigation rather than confirmed disaster or crop-loss assessments.
projectDetails.details:
Cambodia’s changing waters and agricultural landscapes affect communities, livelihoods and infrastructure. However, satellite information can be difficult for non-specialists to access and interpret. A map alone may not explain when a change occurred, which places deserve closer investigation, or how much confidence to place in a result.

SARWATCH makes Earth-observation information easier to explore through an interactive website focused on flooding and agriculture around Tonlé Sap. Our intended users include local planners, disaster-response organizations, agricultural advisers, researchers and students.

What we built

Our Flood Explorer presents 11 team-prepared date layers, labeled from June 19 to October 29, 2026. Users can select dates, swipe between observations, switch between classified water and radar displays, and inspect a first-to-last change layer. The interface also presents team-reported estimates of water area and overlap with population, roads and cropland. These estimates help users identify questions for further investigation; they do not establish confirmed affected people, road closures or crop damage.

A separate reference-filtered open-water view uses a historical JRC water-recurrence reference. We identify this as an exploratory screening proxy rather than a season-matched flood anomaly or operational alert.

Our Agriculture Explorer connects to our teammate-operated API and displays cropland radar-change signals across six Tonlé Sap provinces: Banteay Meanchey, Battambang, Kampong Chhnang, Kampong Thom, Pursat and Siem Reap. Users can select a province, compare the supplied cropland categories, inspect changed-area and valid-coverage figures, and explore rainfall and vegetation charts.

How it addresses Dancing with the SARs

We focus the challenge on a connected Cambodian landscape where water and agriculture interact. SARWATCH turns team-processed radar outputs into dated comparisons, geographic exploration and explanations that users can investigate.

Our interpretation considers possible physical drivers, including seasonal water movement, changing soil moisture, vegetation conditions and agricultural activity. These remain hypotheses requiring supporting evidence. The interface encourages users to distinguish an observed signal from an explanation of its cause.

NASA data and supporting context

The team reports using NISAR radar data obtained through ASF. The agriculture API reports a radar comparison between July 1 and October 17, 2026. NASA MODIS MOD13Q1.061 vegetation outputs, accessed through AppEEARS, provide supplementary historical context. CHIRPS rainfall, ESA WorldCover, WorldPop, OpenStreetMap and JRC Global Surface Water support additional views and reported estimates.

Each source serves a different purpose. Our historical vegetation sample covers December 2020–December 2021 and is presented separately from the 2026 radar comparison. It cannot establish the cause of later radar changes.

Technology and creativity

The website uses Vue 3, TypeScript and Vite, with MapLibre for interactive maps and Three.js for the rotating Earth and transition into Cambodia. The agriculture interface reads structured outputs from our teammate’s API. Charts include accessible data tables, and the application provides loading, missing-data and error states.

Our creative contribution is the combination of an immersive geographic introduction with practical comparisons and visible evidence. Users can move from a global perspective to a local study window, compare observations, inspect province statistics and read the limitations behind each view.

Current limitations and future development

SARWATCH is a working hackathon prototype. Exact radar product identifiers, complete processing documentation, source permissions and independent scientific validation still require further work. Radar changes do not directly establish crop damage or yield loss. The separate synthetic development example is explicitly labeled and is not presented as satellite evidence.

Our next steps are to strengthen product-level provenance, validate classifications and exposure estimates, expand datasets along the Mekong, add contemporary vegetation observations and improve downloadable summaries. Forest monitoring and atmospheric information remain upcoming themes.

AI assistance

We used ChatGPT/Codex to assist with brainstorming, research, interface design, frontend implementation, debugging, integration, documentation and presentation preparation. Our short demo uses AI-assisted editing, captions, motion graphics and an original instrumental soundtrack synthesized through AI-assisted Python code. The video includes a visible acknowledgement and metadata disclosure. A separate synthetic interface-testing fixture is clearly labeled. SARWATCH’s displayed scientific outputs remain team-provided and are not presented as independently validated AI predictions.

projectDetails.name: Echo
projectDetails.summary:
ECHO: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a free 3D Open World game that runs in any web browser, with nothing to download. It makes the story of the objects NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars easy and exciting to learn.
Today, these stories sit in long technical reports written for researchers. In ECHO, you skip the reports and go there. You play a curious student from 2050, when space travel is easy. But long before your time, NASA sent robots and equipment to explore the Moon and Mars, and many are still there. Your mission is to visit them and learn what they achieved.
You walk across the surface, follow a glowing signal to a real NASA machine, and let Echo, your robot guide, scan it. The machine then tells its own story in a short illustrated storybook for grades 6 to 12, in plain language. You inspect its parts in 3D, see the real NASA photo, and answer one quick question to save the story to your archive.
Six levels follow the missions in order, three on the Moon and three on Mars, from the 1960s to today, and each unlocks the next. Every story shows its sources, so curious students can go on to NASA’s own records.
We want students to name these machines, explain their science, and feel closer to real exploration. Next, we will pilot ECHO in 15 Cambodian high schools by the end of 2026 to measure whether students remember mission facts better after playing.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. ECHO is a free 3D game that runs in any browser, with no download. It is a virtual field trip to the machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. We can’t visit them in real life, but in ECHO students can. By creating a fictional story of the year of 2050 where space travel The game has six levels, three on the Moon and three on Mars, from Surveyor 3 to Ingenuity, leading players through Moons and Mars exploration history in chronological order.

How it works. Players walk across the lunar surface and follow glowing signal beams to each machine. Echo, a friendly robot guide, scans the machine and matches it to the archive. Echo then tells the machine’s story as a short illustrated story book, in first person, written for grades 6 to 12. Players inspect the machine’s parts in 3D with an X-ray view, see the real NASA photo, and answer a quick question to save the story in their discovery log. Completing a level unlocks the next one.

Benefits and impact. Students learn what each machine did, what it discovered and how its mission ended, in a way that feels like play instead of reading archive pages. Teachers get a free classroom tool that needs no installation and works on laptops, tablets and phones. We want students to be able to name these machines, explain their science and feel closer to real exploration. Our next step is a pilot with 10 high schools in Cambodia by 2026, and we will measure whether students remember mission facts better after playing.

NASA data and resources. The game uses NASA mission records and NASA photos from NSSDCA (NASA Space Data Coordinated Archive) the NASA Image and Video Library, with source credits shown in the game. We plan to add real terrain from Moon Trek and Mars Trek (LOLA and MOLA elevation) and LROC and HiRISE images. Today the terrain is procedurally generated. 7 available 3D models are taken from the NASA-3D-Resources public repository on github, while the rest are simplified with three.js, not to scale. The game says so on screen and links to the real photo.

Tools. JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Three.js for 3D; Supabase for player accounts and progress; Vercel for hosting. It runs in a web browser on phone, tablet or computer.

Creativity. Instead of showing data, we made the data a place students can walk through. Every machine speaks for itself, and Echo gives students a guide who learns alongside them.

What we considered. Accuracy (every story card is checked against NASA sources), age-appropriate language, low-end school devices, no installation for teachers, and honest labeling of what is simplified.

Use of SI. We used Super Intelligence tools (Claude) to help write and debug parts of the game code, draft story text and presentation copy, and generate some illustrations. All SI-generated images are marked with a visible watermark, and we reviewed and checked the facts against NASA sources.

projectDetails.name: ETIVAQ — See the Sky in Four Dimensions
projectDetails.summary:
ETIVAQ (Exploring Temporal Infrared Variations through Astronomical Queries) is an interactive astronomy platform that connects the night sky we see with the infrared universe observed by NASA's SPHEREx mission.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, ETIVAQ allows users to explore the sky from different locations and times, identify celestial objects, and investigate real NASA infrared observations through an accessible web interface.

Users can navigate a virtual sky, search for astronomical objects, or upload their own night-sky photographs for automated plate solving. They can then explore available SPHEREx observations, compare frames across infrared bands, and examine how astronomical data changes with wavelength and observation time.

ETIVAQ brings together real NASA data, interactive visualization, and citizen exploration in one educational experience.

Our goal extends beyond the hackathon: to develop ETIVAQ into an open-source, community-driven platform where students, educators, amateur astronomers, researchers, and curious individuals can explore and learn together.

The universe belongs to everyone. Exploring it should, too.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem

NASA collects extraordinary amounts of astronomical data, but exploring that information can be challenging for people without specialized scientific knowledge or software.

For many students, educators, and amateur astronomers, there is a disconnect between the night sky they observe and the scientific datasets available through NASA archives.

Our Solution

ETIVAQ bridges that gap by providing an interactive, browser-based astronomy exploration platform.

Rather than presenting astronomical data as a collection of files, ETIVAQ allows users to begin with something familiar: the night sky itself.

How ETIVAQ Works

1. Explore the Night Sky

Users can navigate an interactive sky map, select their observing location, adjust the date and time, and discover celestial objects. The platform incorporates horizon and directional information to connect the virtual sky with real-world observation.

2. Find Your Photograph in Space

Users can upload their own night-sky photographs. ETIVAQ integrates Astrometry.net plate-solving services to identify the photographed sky region and connect it with the interactive map.

3. Explore NASA SPHEREx Data

Users can select a sky position and access available SPHEREx observations through NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

4. Investigate Infrared Observations

The SPHEREx viewer provides tools for exploring individual frames, detector bands, observation sequences, image stacking, difference visualization, and quality-based frame rejection.

These features support visual exploration while clearly distinguishing educational comparisons from scientifically validated measurements.

Technology and Resources

ETIVAQ uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, Aladin Lite, Astrometry.net, and NASA/IPAC IRSA services.

The platform incorporates astronomical coordinate transformations, interactive sky visualization, image-processing functions, and FITS-based scientific data handling.

What Makes ETIVAQ Different?

ETIVAQ connects three experiences that are often separated: observing the night sky, identifying celestial objects, and exploring scientific infrared data.

Users do not need to begin by understanding FITS files, astronomical coordinate systems, or archive query interfaces. They can start by looking at the sky.

Intended Impact

ETIVAQ aims to make NASA astronomical data more accessible to students, educators, amateur astronomers, and the general public.

Our long-term vision is to develop ETIVAQ as an open-source, community-driven educational platform that supports further scientific exploration, public outreach, localization, and contributions from developers and astronomy enthusiasts worldwide.

ETIVAQ was developed as a collaborative project combining astronomy research, software development, user experience design, and AI-assisted development under the direction of Team ETIVAQ.

projectDetails.name: Project Five Little Space Monkeys
projectDetails.summary: Our game aims to help children, particularly teenagers with an interest in space, explore their passions in a fun, engaging, and inexpensive way. According to our research, we identified a gap in opportunities for aspiring individuals to gain hands-on experience before entering their desired fields. Although many may be interested in pursuing space-related careers, there are inadequate accessible opportunities to practice and develop relevant skills beforehand. Our game aims to fill this void by providing an interactive learning environment where space enthusiasts can experiment, practice, and explore different aspects of space missions. Players start by defining their objectives, followed by designing a spacecraft. Throughout the game, players will be met with different tasks and space-related challenges. By simulating the process of designing a space mission, users will have the ability to enhance their proficiency in different operational segments of the mission: managing limited budgets, power, mass, and launch vehicles with help from accurate NASA data, while also fostering foundational skills and responsibilities involved in having a shot at these types of careers. As students ourselves, we understand other students’ needs. Therefore, we crafted a launchpad for them to initiate their exploration, turning today's space enthusiasts into potential future aerospace specialists.
projectDetails.details:
The outcome of our project is an interactive space mission simulation game that allows students to experience the process of designing and operating a complete space mission. To bring this idea to life, we utilized tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and CodeSandbox as our guide to develop the game using HTML and JavaScript. In addition, we also referred to NASA's educational and scientific resources like NASA – Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators, NASA – How Far Away Is the Moon?, etc. These resources were used to ensure the accuracy of the different information used in our game such as spacecraft power systems, the distance between Earth and the Moon, Europa as a potential destination for scientific exploration (NASA – Europa), the characteristics of Mars (NASA – Mars), and the environmental conditions of Venus (NASA – Venus Facts). 

When players first join the server, they will be introduced to the process of defining a mission's objectives and requirements. From there, they will progress to designing their spacecraft, which involves managing scientific instruments and making decisions about other essential mission components, such as the launcher and orbiter. Beyond spacecraft design, players must also manage limited resources, including budget, mass, power, communications, and data. This aids in acclimating them to the procedures involved in planning a successful space mission. Furthermore, our game supports up to four participants, giving players the opportunity to collaborate, just as they would when working as a team in real life. As the game progresses, different challenges and problems will arise according to the work that the team has done. This will help point out the different loopholes that the team may have missed, creating a reaction loop that would help the players develop more awareness about the consequences of their actions. Ultimately, our project aims to provide more than just an entertaining gaming experience. We aim to plant the seeds in students, inspiring them to pursue space careers while also providing them with the nourishment they need to build a strong foundation to sprout into a towering tree in the future.
