projectDetails.name: FlameLens SI
projectDetails.summary:
For decades NASA has studied how fire behaves in microgravity. The results sit in the PSI archive as 24 investigations and 25 data tables, each with its own columns, units and abbreviations. NASA's challenge says this volume makes them "hard to find, compare, and understand," and asks for an interactive, SI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets them.

FlameLens SI is that dashboard, live at flamelens.si. It turns NASA's tables into clear answers. It summarizes all 24 investigations in plain words. It ranks them for any crew cabin an engineer describes. It interprets: a student asks the SI a question and can check every number in the answer, and a professor shows the class NASA's own video of the nearest real test. Behind it is one clean table of 2,143 tests and 28,316 values, each traced to its NASA file, row and column.

The result is fire safety insight for human space exploration that an engineer, a professor or a student can read in seconds. One example: NASA expects the Moon Base to hold 30% oxygen or more, and the dashboard shows at a glance that the open archive has no fabric or plastic test above 22.7% oxygen.
projectDetails.details:
TRY IT IN ONE MINUTE (no login)

1. Open https://flamelens.si/explore?tour=1 for a guided tour of the dashboard, or open https://flamelens.si and press "Open the dashboard".

2. Choose "Lunar surface habitat" and press "Analyze this cabin". The grid counts NASA's tests by fuel and oxygen, and shows the empty squares where the evidence stops.

3. Open the Flame Lab and press play. You are watching NASA's own recording of the nearest real test.

4. Ask the SI: "Has anything been tested at 34% oxygen?" The answer lists its lookups, its sources and a check of every number.

If flamelens.si is blocked on your network, the same site is at https://flamelens-staging.vercel.app

Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/kavatana/flamelens-si

FROM NASA'S TABLES TO CLEAR ANSWERS

In NASA's table, one test is a row of cells such as "SIBAL 2 cm" and "=171.81/756.14". In FlameLens SI the same test reads: cotton and fiberglass fabric, burned in 22.7% oxygen, the highest oxygen any solid in the archive was tested in. NASA's original cell is shown beside every value, so nothing is hidden and anyone can check it.

WHO IT IS FOR, AND WHAT EACH ONE GETS

- The aerospace engineer designing a lunar habitat. She enters the cabin's air (34% oxygen, 56.5 kPa) and the fabric of its seats. In seconds the Dashboard shows that NASA's open archive has no fabric test near that air, names the closest test that does exist, and ranks the investigations worth reading first. A gap found on day one becomes a test requested before the design is fixed.

- The aerospace researcher planning the next experiment. One grid shows every test by fuel and oxygen, with empty squares where nothing was run. The Data view exports every row, with its source, ready for a model.

- The professor teaching combustion. He opens the Flame Lab, picks a plastic rod, lowers the oxygen, and the class watches NASA's own recording of a real flame on the space station, beside the curves NASA measured while it burned.

- The graduate or undergraduate student. Each of the 24 investigations is explained in plain words. The student asks the SI a question by typing or speaking, and can check every number in the answer against NASA's source.

- And on Earth. What is learned in a sealed cabin helps submarines, aircraft and other closed spaces.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

NASA asked for an SI-powered dashboard that "summarizes, ranks, and interprets" the PSI combustion investigations, and named three things users should be able to do. FlameLens SI does each one.

1. "Identify investigations most relevant to the fire safety needs of habitable crew environments."

The Dashboard. Pick a space station, a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover or a spacesuit, or set your own oxygen, pressure, gravity and material. It ranks the 24 investigations for that cabin, counts the tests close to its air, and marks where the evidence runs out.

2. "Extract data that supports predictive modeling of flammability and fire scenarios."

The Data view. Every test row can be filtered and downloaded as CSV or JSON. Each value carries its unit, its NASA source and a label that says whether NASA reported it, NASA's text states it, or it was assumed, so a modeller knows exactly what they are fitting to.

3. "Highlight research that informs the development of next-generation fire safety controls and equipment."

The Safety view. It groups the research by NASA's own three jobs (prevention, detection and suppression), with what each investigation found and NASA's sentence that says so.

It also covers what NASA suggested teams consider:

- Summaries of each investigation: objectives, fuels with their shape and size, oxygen, pressure and air speed, what was varied between tests, and the sensors used.

- Similarities and differences: any investigations side by side, and one grid of every test by fuel and oxygen.

- Fire safety on Earth: how this research reached firefighter air tanks, smoke detectors and protective clothing.

- Every audience NASA names: engineers and researchers get the data and its sources; professors and students get real NASA flames in plain words.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT IT

- It plays NASA's own recording of the test. 479 tests have a NASA video, streamed straight from NASA's storage, next to the curves NASA measured while the test burned (448,551 points) and 1,819 NASA photographs.

- It reads NASA's reports as well as NASA's tables. From the tables alone, only 11 solid-fuel tests have oxygen, air speed and an outcome together. With NASA's reports and test sheets, 212 do, and each added value quotes NASA's own sentence.

- It keeps NASA's original cell beside every value. The highest oxygen for a solid in the archive, 22.7%, comes from a cell in NASA's BASS spreadsheet written as a formula: 171.81 / 756.14, oxygen pressure over total pressure. Anyone can open the test and see it.

- It does not predict and it does not grade. Where NASA has no test, it says "not known" and names the nearest real test, instead of estimating a flame or scoring a cabin as safe.

- You can talk to it. Questions can be spoken, and answers can be read aloud.

HOW IT WORKS

1. A Python pipeline reads NASA's 25 PSI data tables and NASA's reports and test sheets, and cleans them into one table. Names and units are made the same across experiments.

2. Every value keeps NASA's original cell beside it, the column it came from, and a label: reported, read from NASA's text (quoted), assumed (with the reason), or corrected (original kept).

3. The table is stored in Postgres. The website draws every page, chart and count from it.

4. The SI assistant is a language model that can only call four lookups on that table: search the tests, read one experiment, find tests near a cabin's air, and search NASA's text. It has no internet access. After it answers, code checks every number against what the lookups returned and flags any number it cannot back up.

5. NASA's videos are not copied. The site asks NASA's archive for a short-lived link and the video plays straight from NASA's storage.

WHY IT CAN BE TRUSTED

- Counts, charts and rankings are computed by code, never written by the model.

- Where two NASA files disagree, both values are kept side by side (59 places). Missing values stay "not reported" and are never treated as zero.

- The site ranks relevance. It never rates a cabin as safe.

- If the model service is down, the site still answers from prepared answers and NASA's own text.

- More than 300 automated tests cover the site and the pipeline, and the live site was tested with 250 visitors at once.

- Its limits are stated on the site at https://flamelens.si/methods

WHAT WE FOUND

- In NASA's open PSI archive, no fabric or plastic was burned above 22.7% oxygen. NASA's challenge states that the Moon Base will likely be at 30% oxygen or greater.

- No combustion test in the archive ran at Moon or Mars gravity. The challenge statement confirms that PSI holds no partial-gravity data yet.

- 1,121 tests have more than a table row: measured curves, photographs or NASA's own sentences.

WHAT IS NEXT

Add NASA's partial-gravity results (for example from LUCI and FM2) as soon as they are published, add more of NASA's flame-spread and smoke data, and ask fire-safety experts to review the readings.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Python (pandas, pydantic, PyYAML, openpyxl, pytest, uv) for the data pipeline. TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, three.js, d3-scale, mpegts.js, Zod, Drizzle and Postgres for the site. Hosted on Vercel with a Neon Postgres database. The SI assistant runs on Amazon Bedrock (gpt-oss-120b). Answers can be read aloud with ElevenLabs.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

Each use is also stated on the site (https://flamelens.si/methods), in the page metadata, in the repository's README and in the JSON export.

- Code and text: the code, the data pipeline and the site's text were written with an SI coding tool (Claude, Anthropic), working with the team.

- Reading the investigations: the one-line summaries, fire-safety levels and ratings of the 24 investigations were written by an SI after reading each PSI record. Each carries a quotation from NASA, and the build stops if a quotation is not found word for word in NASA's text.

- Answering questions on the site: a language model on Amazon Bedrock (gpt-oss-120b). It can only run four fixed lookups, and every number it writes is checked against the data.

- Audio: the Listen button reads an answer aloud with an SI voice (ElevenLabs). The demo video's narration, music and sound effects were also generated with ElevenLabs.

- Images and video: the line drawings of cabins and fire-safety jobs, their short animations and two turnable concept models were made with image and video models through Higgsfield. Each carries a visible "SI-generated" mark, and none contains a NASA logo, flag or mission badge. Every photograph and all footage of flames are NASA's own.

- Demo video: NASA's own footage of a spherical flame (CFI-G, from the PSI archive) and a screen recording of the live site. Its title cards and editing were made with scripts written by an SI coding tool. Its SI-generated sound is stated on its last frame, on its page and in the file's metadata.

- Not used for the numbers: no value in the tables, charts or ranking was produced or estimated by a model. Each comes from a PSI table cell or from NASA's own text, through code.

NASA DATA USED

- NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive, https://psi.nasa.gov : the records, experimental data tables, reports, test matrices, ReadMe files, photographs and video recordings of 24 combustion investigations: Flame Design (PSI-10), BRE (PSI-20), CLD Flame (PSI-21), E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22), s-Flame (PSI-23), BASS-II (PSI-25), BASS (PSI-26), CFI (PSI-39), DAFT (PSI-47), SPICE soot analysis (PSI-60), BASS flame-spread modelling (PSI-62), FLEX-2 (PSI-68), FLEX (PSI-69), Saffire-I (PSI-98), Saffire-II (PSI-99), Saffire-III (PSI-100), SAME-R (PSI-101), SAME (PSI-102), SLICE (PSI-106), SPICE (PSI-107), SAME smoke modelling (PSI-115), Cool-flame CFD (PSI-117), Cool-flame transitions (PSI-142) and CFI-G (PSI-159).

- NASA's challenge statement and resources for "Flame in Freefall": the crew atmospheres (Moon Base at 30% oxygen or greater and 10.2 psi or less; spacesuit at 100% oxygen and 4.3 psi), NASA's Combustion Science pages, the Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science, and NASA's accounts of Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and the Mir fire.

- NASA Spinoff pages on firefighter air tanks (1976), the fire detector (1978) and protective clothing (1982), for the Earth applications.

- NASA 3D models on the home page: Earth and Mars (NASA Science 3D resources, NASA/JPL-Caltech), the Moon (NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data) and the International Space Station (NASA's ISS model).

OTHER DATA AND CREDITS

No Space Agency Partner data was used. Every photograph and every recording of a flame is NASA's, credited where it appears. No other third-party images, music or text are used. Fonts: IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono (SIL Open Font License). SI image and video models, used through Higgsfield: FLUX.2, Seedance 2.5, Nano Banana Pro and GPT Image 2.6.

projectDetails.name: FieldWise Cambodia
projectDetails.summary:
FieldWise Cambodia is a decision-support prototype that helps Cambodian farmers and agricultural advisers explore what to plant next as part of crop-rotation planning. Users select a field, indicate water access and their current crop, and compare three next-crop candidates with explanations, supporting evidence, and information gaps.

The web app combines NASA POWER rainfall and seasonal climate context with local land-cover and surface-water information and agricultural rotation rules. Landsat, SRTM, and NASA EONET provide additional observational and risk context when available. A companion Telegram bot aims to make agricultural information more accessible to farmers facing literacy barriers.

Farmer interviews and field observations in Saang informed our understanding of planting decisions, including water conditions, soil concerns, market uncertainty, and access to knowledge. FieldWise makes the reasoning behind crop comparisons visible while preserving farmer judgment. Agronomic validation and further usability testing are needed before practical field recommendations.
projectDetails.details:
FieldWise Cambodia helps farmers and agricultural advisers explore what to plant next as part of crop-rotation planning. It connects environmental observations with agricultural knowledge and basic information about a farmer’s situation, making the reasoning behind crop comparisons visible.

The problem we address

Choosing the next crop involves more than environmental suitability. Farmers also consider selling opportunities, available funds, water access, previous crops, and experience. During our hackathon field visit in Saang, farmers described concerns involving water and flooding, soil conditions, pests, unpredictable prices, and access to agricultural knowledge. These conversations informed our problem framing. They represent local experiences rather than findings that can be generalized to all Cambodian farmers.

How the prototype works

Users select a location on a map of Cambodia, indicate whether they have access to their own water supply, and choose their current crop. The web app returns three next-crop candidates. Users can open a candidate to examine why it appears, the contributing comparison factors, supporting observations, information gaps, and risks requiring local review.

The prototype supports exploration of crop transitions relevant to rotation planning. Further development is needed to evaluate complete multi-season rotation strategies.

How NASA data contributes

NASA POWER provides rainfall and seasonal climate context, including comparisons with a 2001–2020 historical baseline. Rainfall contributes directly to the prototype’s crop-matching rules.

SRTM elevation data provides slope and terrain context. Landsat observations support interpretation of vegetation and exposed soil when usable imagery is available. NASA EONET provides context on reported natural events when the feed is accessible. Missing observations remain visible to users.

Local context includes SERVIR-Mekong/CDE land-cover information, JRC Global Surface Water, and agricultural rotation rules. Thea’s crop reference draws on Helen Keller International/Cambodia’s 2003 home-gardening handbook. Its guidance requires review against current local conditions.

Accessible information

Alongside the web app, we developed a Telegram bot intended to make agricultural information more accessible to farmers facing literacy barriers. Our intended users include agricultural advisers, trainers, and community leaders who can help farmers interpret the information.

Web prototype
https://fieldwise-tfhvwxa77q-an.a.run.app/map/b.html

Telegram bot
https://t.me/FieldWise_bot

What makes the approach useful

FieldWise brings environmental evidence and agricultural guidance into a location-based comparison. Users can see the reasons behind a candidate and identify what still needs checking. The combination of a visual map, explainable comparisons, and a companion Telegram channel explores different ways to make Earth observation information usable in farming discussions.

Validation and limitations

We conducted farmer interviews and field observations during the hackathon and built a functioning web prototype. This establishes an initial proof of concept. It does not establish agronomic accuracy, farmer usability, or improvements in yields, income, or soil health.

Match scores reflect prototype rules. They are not probabilities of crop success. NASA POWER provides regional context at approximately 50-kilometre resolution and cannot describe rainfall or soil conditions on an individual plot. Satellite observations also cannot establish seed availability, household resources, market access, or irrigation reliability.

Our next steps are to review the crop rules with agricultural specialists, test both interfaces with farmers and advisers, verify local crop and market information, and expand coverage as supporting evidence becomes available. Our intended impact is to help people discuss rotation options with a clearer understanding of their evidence, trade-offs, and uncertainties.

projectDetails.name: Investigating Japan's earthquakes using NISAR data
projectDetails.summary: We developed a website, with the purpose of visualizing the earthquake magnitudes in Japan, incorporating timestamps that allows everyone to view the earthquake's changes over time. Using data from UAVSAR and external sources, we were able to design a website that enables all users to observe the difference in magnitudes that has affected different areas (such as Hokkaido, Tohoku, Kanto, Kyushu...) in Japan, throughout the years. This is crucial for everyone to be aware of the changes of earth's tectonic plates and how frequent earthquakes - from light tremors to deadly destructions - has become for Japan.
projectDetails.details:
The website provides different settings for it's users to tweak to their liking, such as a precise adjustable time stamp/time player, managing data ranging from either 1-12months. Moreover it can filter out different regions of preference, likewise, it has an intuitive color explanation for an easy understanding.

We acknowledge that there are live websites that constantly update earthquake magnitudes in Japan, however, our site offers dynamic visuals and flexibility as users are able to filter different areas, and their desirable way to view seismic changes.

Our intended impact is to raise awareness about how frequent Japan’s earthquakes have become, it’s noticed that they have become more persistent over time, despite lower magnitudes. Since it also updates regularly, people can be informed of the latest information, while collaborating to develop solutions to protect others.

The website is built in Visual Studio Code, using API, Python and numerous libraries (Streamlit, Pandas, Numpy, Plotly, requests, and steamlit-autorefresh).

Our website has both light and dark modes, which everyone can change based on their preferences, our time-lapse also offers two different filters: cumulative or simply event-by-event, with data ranging from 1897 to the present. Other than magnitude levels, users can also view the depth of each earthquake, which means how deep the impact has caused, and allows us to magnify to different areas of the country, giving more detailed views. additionally, it’s user-friendly since it’s simple to understand and has key terms to guide people on how to interpret the information.

Our website explores three key factors. Firstly, accessibility, we vision our website to reach worldwide, and allow everyone to gain awareness about earthquakes, and make sure it’s comprehensible. Secondly, simplicity, our website should be neat and simple to use, including guidance in our website to help people navigate through it easily. Lastly, speed, we made sure it was quick-paced and constant so people don’t miss out on any new information.

projectDetails.name: Space Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
What remains when humanity's greatest space mission is over? Beyond what humanity has discovered they leave behind extraordinary machines that once carried our curiosity beyond Earth, yet their stories are often forgotten.
	
	Welcome to Space Legacy, an interactive 3D educational platform developed to bring the stories of NASA’s forgotten space exploration hardware back to life. Throughout the platform the users can explore the Moon, Mars as well as the rest of the solar system. Users can also discover abandoned spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific equipment, and learn about the past missions. 

    Rather than simply present the historical face, Space Legacy uses interactive 3D environments, mission replay, visual storytelling, and educational information to help the user understand how those machinery and missions operated. Follow different stages of the space missions, from launching to landing in an engaging  storytelling from the narrator. 

   Space Legacy was designed specifically for the school-age students who are enthusiastic about space exploration. Transform complex scientific and historical information into accessible and immersive learning experiences. Who hopes Space Legacy will remind everyone that even though the mission ends, its discoveries and contribution continue to shape humanity's understanding of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem We Address

Space exploration is often remembered through its greatest discoveries, successful missions, and scientific achievements. However, the machines and equipment are often overlooked once their missions are complete. Their purposes, engineering designs, and contributions to science deserve to be remembered and understood.

Space Legacy will address this gap by transforming the stories of forgotten space equipment into an interactive experience where people can explore, learn, and appreciate the technology.

Vision and Mission 

Our Vision

To make the stories of space exploration accessible to everyone, inspiring people of all ages, especially young learners, to discover the wonders of space, appreciate human achievements, and imagine the possibilities of future exploration.

Our Mission

From stories of forgotten space equipment into engaging and easy-to-understand learning experiences through interactive storytelling, 3D visualizations, authentic NASA images, and real scientific data. We aim to make space history and science enjoyable, accessible, and meaningful for everyone.

Browse Mission

The Browse Missions section organizes space exploration into six destination-based categories making the user experience easier to discover the mission according to the region.  These categories include Earth Orbit, the Moon, Mars, the Sun, Mercury & Venus, Outer Planets & Beyond, and Asteroids & Comets. 

In the same Browse Mission tab, it has a Hardware Explorer which contains 64 space exploration objects, organized into seven hardware categories: Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Telescopes, Landers & Rovers, Scientific Instruments, Space Stations, and Return Capsules.

Throughout this section users can navigate different parts of the Solar System and select individual objects to explore the 3D model. This organization will help the users understand the mission’s contribution to our understanding of space and the technologies role involved in space exploration.

Mission Replay

The Mission Replay system allows users to experience selected historical missions through a sequence of interactive 3D scenes.

Each replay follows the actual stages relevant to that mission, rather than using one generic animation for every spacecraft. Depending on the mission, users can experience:

  • Launch and rocket liftoff.
  • Rocket stage separation and orbit insertion.
  • Interplanetary travel and spacecraft maneuvers.
  • Landing, orbital arrival, or equipment deployment.
  • Return to Earth and splashdown, where applicable.
  • Mission completion and final status.

A timeline, narration, captions, and playback controls help users follow the events and understand their significance.

Mission Simulator — Engineering Bay

The Engineering Bay allows users to experiment with the engineering decisions involved in building a space mission. It provides two modes:

Free Build (Sandbox Mode): Users can experiment with different components and create their own mission configurations. Combinations that have never flown are clearly identified as fictional.

This feature also introduces users to the importance of mission compatibility. Briefing explains potential limitations of the user's custom mission configuration  to the real engineering performance data. 

Astronaut Exploration &  AI Astronaut Assistance

After completing a simulated mission, users can continue into an interactive lunar or Martian environment.

Users can explore selected historical landing regions, move around as astronauts, operate vehicles, investigate scientific targets, and discover objects associated with previous missions.

The experience includes:

  • Walking, running, and jumping with movement adapted to the gravity of different worlds.
  • Driving the Lunar Roving Vehicle in selected Apollo landing environments.
  • Exploring Mars rover environments and interacting with scientific targets.
  • Recording discoveries, taking photographs, and collecting information about historical objects.

Another special function during the navigation of the region, the users will have AI Astronaut Assistance acts as their virtual guide throughout the experience. Rather than simply exploring the environment, users can learn the stories behind the objects they encounter through AI-powered storytelling.

My Collection 

This is the users collection from their past Mission Simulator. This will provide a revisit collected objects, read their information card, review the photographs and track their exploration progress. 

"While we explore new worlds, Space Legacy preserves the stories of those who came before." - KAMPU SPACE

NASA Data and Scientific Resources

Space Legacy uses NASA's scientific resources, mission records. By incorporating authentic NASA datasets and imagery, we aim to turn scientific information into accessible visual and interactive learning experiences.

NASA's resources also help us maintain historical accuracy and ensure that the stories presented throughout Space Legacy are supported by reliable evidence.

Tool, Technologies and Development

Space Legacy was developed as a browser-based application using the following technologies:

The project currently uses vanilla JavaScript ES modules and a Three.js CDN import map, without requiring a separate build process. 

Intended Impact

Our goal is to make the history and achievements of space exploration more accessible, engaging, and meaningful to everyone. We hope Space Legacy will encourage students to develop an interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), while raising awareness about the abandoned technology and equipment in outer space.

projectDetails.name: MOONDA
projectDetails.summary:
The Moon's south pole the Sun never rises more than 1.5degrees above the horizon, so with a single hill it can leave the robot in darkness for days without solar power or hide it from Earth, inadvertently cut off radio link and signal. Choosing where and when to land decides if the mission will succeed or not. 

Meet Moonda, a google earth for moon, that answers questions directly about moon landing. Drop pins on any location within the moon, and Moonda will give you all the data you need from sunlight access over a period of days, service communication to earth, highlighted crates, water molecules present and even danger zones indicating height differences on the moon surface. In addition to that we have a built in AI that can predict different landing regions and predict travel routes. Moonda also offers an immersive experience with a 3D look as the rover. Moonda is a Cambodian product, we offer languages in English and Khmer. The app localizes through timeline with the international time frame UTC and the Cambodia local time GMT+7

This is important because it shows the unique features that align with our intended audience of both mission planners and the public. With different options from 3D experience to 2D image, our app is accessible by everyone.
projectDetails.details:
MOONDA is an interactive 3D Moon where you can explore the lunar surface and test landing sites. You can search 9,087 official IAU names, NASA's nine Artemis regions, and 76 past or planned mission sites, or click anywhere. Once you pick a spot and arrival date, our code scans 720 directions along the curved surface using NASA LOLA heights to find the tallest hills and build a local skyline. Then, Astronomy Engine tracks where the Sun and Earth are at every step of the mission. Whenever either drops below the skyline, a hill is blocking it. MOONDA turns this into a daily timeline showing total sunlight, longest darkness, Earth visibility, and longest time without contact. Our Sun and Earth positions match NASA/JPL Horizons within 0.0014°, and famous spots match real data: Shackleton crater's floor gets 0% sunlight, while Connecting Ridge gets around 80%.

How MOONDA AI works

MOONDA AI works as an agent rather than a normal chatbot. The language model figures out what you are asking and explains the results, while our own code does the actual science through seven custom tools like analyse_spot and scan_area. When someone asks for the sunniest spot near a crater, the AI runs these tools on real NASA data and gets back the true numbers. Its rules forbid making up any number that didn't come from a tool, and every tool call shows up on screen.

NASA data and who it helps

Along with LOLA heights, MOONDA uses LROC images, Diviner temperatures and ice predictions, permanent-shadow maps, LCROSS and M3 water evidence, and the Robbins crater catalogue. It turns complicated NASA files into clear answers anyone can understand in seconds. Student teams and small space groups can quickly check a site, students in Cambodia can explore real NASA science in Khmer even offline, and anyone following Artemis can see why landing location and timing matter.

How we built it

We coded MOONDA in TypeScript with React, Vite, and CesiumJS, running heavy math in Web Workers so the 3D Moon stays smooth. Python scripts using NumPy and rasterio turned gigabytes of NASA files into small tiles that load on demand. MOONDA AI uses the DeepSeek API, and the site is hosted on Netlify. We built everything in VS Code with Git and GitHub, using Claude and Codex as coding helpers while our team defined the problem, checked the datasets, designed the interface, and verified the results.

Design choices and scientific limits

Tools like LROC QuickMap only show map layers, while MOONDA answers the real planning question for a specific spot, date, and mission length, and lets you stand on the ground to watch the Sun move along the horizon. We made sure to keep the science honest: permanently shadowed areas are labeled as cold traps instead of confirmed ice, "Earth in view" means line of sight rather than a guaranteed signal, and rocks near the rover are marked as an artist's impression. We also added a tutorial, Khmer translation, offline mode, and full credits for every dataset.

projectDetails.name: FlameX: NASA Fire Research for Cambodia's Space Generation
projectDetails.summary:
FlameX (flamex.study) turns NASA's scattered microgravity combustion research into one free, easy-to-use web platform. NASA has run decades of fire experiments in space, but the results are spread across 24 investigations and 66,602 files written for scientists. Cambodia is preparing its first satellite but has no facilities to run its own microgravity fire experiments.

FlameX brings 1,095 real NASA tests and 142 NASA documents into one place. Users can explore the data, simulate how flames ignite, spread and go out using three validated machine-learning models, and ask questions in plain language with answers cited to the exact NASA page. Every prediction shows its accuracy, warns when it goes beyond NASA's tested conditions, and lists the nearest real experiments. FlameX also shows what NASA has never tested, such as solid materials in Moon-base air.

It helps Cambodian students, researchers and engineers learn from space research, and carries its fire-safety lessons back to Earth.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameX is a web platform that makes NASA's microgravity fire research easy to find, understand and use. It has five main tools:

- Explore: 1,095 real NASA tests in one searchable table, with key findings, coverage maps and links to every NASA source.

- Simulator: predicts whether a gas leak ignites, whether a droplet flame goes out, and how fast fire spreads on a solid, using validated machine-learning models.

- Test room: users build their own virtual experiment in a microgravity chamber and watch it run.

- Scenario lab: ranks NASA experiments for a habitat (ISS, Moon base, Mars) and shows which conditions were never tested.

- Ask: answers questions in plain language from 142 NASA documents, citing the exact page.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: we downloaded NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data through its API (24 investigations). Five investigations had per-test tables (ACME CFI-G, ACME Flame Design, FLEX, BASS-II, Saffire-II). We cleaned them into one table of 1,095 tests with consistent units. For BASS-II we also extracted spread rates and crew observations from NASA's technical report, and measured flame spread from ISS video to check our pipeline. Our result matched NASA's published trend.

2. Models: we compared 36 candidate models using grouped cross-validation (tests from the same day never appear in both training and testing) and a physics check (more oxygen must never make ignition less likely). Three passed: Random Forest for gas ignition (ROC-AUC 0.76), a neural network for droplet extinction (ROC-AUC 0.91) and a log-log regression for spread rate (R² 0.93). A fourth model, for whether a solid flame goes out by itself, could not beat a coin flip (AUC 0.51) because NASA's data has only 9 burn-to-end cases, so we report it as a data gap instead of using it.

3. Ask: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over 10,364 passages from 142 NASA documents. The language model only answers from retrieved NASA text, and an automatic check flags any number that does not appear in the sources.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Students and researchers can learn space fire science from real data without a space lab.

- Every answer is traceable to a NASA source, and every prediction warns when it goes beyond the tested data.

- The gap map shows what NASA has never tested, for example no solid material has been burned in Moon-base air (30% oxygen or more), giving researchers clear topics for future work.

- Cambodia is preparing its first satellite. FlameX helps a new space nation learn from existing NASA data instead of repeating expensive experiments, and brings fire-safety lessons back to Earth, where more than 900,000 Cambodians work in garment factories.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Honesty built into the interface: accuracy scores, out-of-range warnings, nearest real tests, and a number check on AI answers.

- It shows what is missing, not only what is known.

- A hands-on test room where anyone can design a microgravity fire experiment.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python, pandas, scikit-learn, Jupyter notebooks, PyMuPDF and pypdf (NASA report parsing), FastAPI, React and TypeScript with Vite, ECharts, Docker, Google Gemini API and Ollama (gemma3:4b) for the Ask feature.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific validity (grouped cross-validation, physics checks, comparison with NASA's published results), transparency (every number links to its source), honest limits (data gaps reported, not hidden), accessibility for non-experts, and running offline on a normal laptop with a local language model.

Team NASA Sakha Kampuchea, Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

projectDetails.name: ORBY: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer – A 90-Day Lunar Survival Simulation
projectDetails.summary:
ORBY is an interactive lunar mission simulation designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of living and working on the Moon. Inspired by NASA's Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, the project places players in charge of a four-person astronaut crew completing a 90-day lunar mission.

Players must manage essential resources, including oxygen, water, food, energy, fuel, and emergency supplies, while responding to environmental hazards, equipment failures, and unexpected mission events. Each astronaut has a specialized role, encouraging teamwork, strategic thinking, and decision-making.

ORBY incorporates NASA scientific resources related to lunar terrain, sunlight, temperature, space weather, radiation, astronaut health, and plant growth to support realistic mission scenarios. Through interactive gameplay, children can explore space science, understand the difficulties of lunar exploration, and learn why resource management and teamwork are essential for future Moon missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

ORBY is an interactive 90-day lunar mission simulation inspired by NASA's Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. It is designed for children aged 7–12 to explore the responsibilities and challenges of living on the Moon through an engaging, educational experience.

The simulation places players in charge of a crew of four astronauts. Each astronaut has a specialized responsibility, and players must work together to keep the lunar outpost operational throughout the mission.

How Does It Work?

Players experience different mission scenarios and make decisions that affect the survival and success of their crew.

The main gameplay systems include:

  • Resource Management: Monitor and manage oxygen, water, food, fuel, energy, and emergency supplies.
  • Power Management: Balance solar energy, battery reserves, and essential equipment during periods of limited sunlight.
  • Crew Health: Monitor astronaut health and respond to medical situations.
  • Lunar Exploration: Explore the lunar surface, study terrain, and collect geological samples.
  • Hydroponics: Manage plant growth and water consumption to support food production.
  • Mission Emergencies: Respond to equipment failures, radiation hazards, resource shortages, and unexpected events.

Each astronaut has a dedicated role:

  1. Pilot – Supports navigation, exploration, and mission operations.
  2. Geologist – Studies lunar terrain and collects geological samples.
  3. Flight Engineer – Manages power systems and life-support equipment.
  4. Medical Officer – Monitors crew health and medical emergencies.

NASA Data and Scientific Foundation

A major part of ORBY is connecting gameplay with real scientific information and NASA resources.

Our team researched and collected resources from several NASA science programs and missions, including:

  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) terrain and elevation data.
  • Lunar illumination and sunlight maps.
  • Diviner lunar surface temperature observations.
  • NASA DONKI historical space-weather records.
  • NASA RadLab lunar-orbit radiation measurements.
  • NASA OSDR astronaut health and spaceflight plant-growth datasets.
  • NASA life-support and lunar solar-energy research.

These resources provide scientific references for designing lunar environmental conditions, resource-management scenarios, crew health systems, radiation hazards, and hydroponics mechanics.

Where real measurements are unavailable or unsuitable for direct gameplay use, simulated values are used for educational scenarios rather than presented as actual scientific measurements.

Tools and Technologies

The project is developed as a web-based interactive simulation and hosted through Vercel.

The development process involves web development technologies, programming, data preparation, and scientific research. NASA datasets are collected and organized to support the simulation's different gameplay systems.

Programming Languages

  • TypeScript (strict mode) — entire game engine, UI, and data pipeline
  • Python — offline data normalization scripts (NASA dataset ingestion only; no server at runtime)
  • CSS (Tailwind CSS v4 utility classes + custom design tokens)

Frameworks & Libraries

  • React 19 — UI component tree and state management
  • Vite — build tooling and dev server
  • Three.js (WebGL2) — custom 3D scene engine (GameEngine.ts), lunar surface, astronaut models, solar system orrery
  • postprocessing — real-time visual effects: UnrealBloom, Vignette, Chromatic Aberration, ACES Filmic Tone Mapping, SMAA anti-aliasing
  • Lucide React — iconography
  • Web Audio API — 100% procedural, synthesized spatial audio (telemetry beeps, suit breathing, radio comms); zero audio files

Data & APIs

  • NASA DONKI — real solar particle event flux (mSv/hr) driving the solar storm crisis mechanic
  • NASA OSDR (OSD-575, OSD-655) — crew blood/cytokine data for the medical officer; VEG-04 hydroponic yield data
  • NASA NTRS (20210011743) — VSAT solar array specs (45 kW peak); BVAD crew resource consumption rates
  • NASA LRO WAC + CRaTER — lunar geology surface data and radiation measurements
  • LCROSS ice data — research yield multiplier (1.56×) for ice-rich terrain

Hosting & Deployment

  • Vercel — static deployment, zero backend at runtime (all game logic runs client-side in the browser)
  • Render - backend

Development Tools

  • Git + GitHub
  • Bun — script runner and test runner

Creativity and Innovation

ORBY combines space exploration, resource management, science education, and decision-making into one interactive mission experience.

Instead of simply teaching children facts about space, the simulation allows them to experience the consequences of their decisions. For example, reducing available power may require the crew to prioritize life-support systems over scientific activities.

The four specialized astronaut roles also encourage collaboration and demonstrate how different responsibilities contribute to mission success.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to make space science more accessible and interesting to young learners.

ORBY encourages children to develop scientific curiosity, critical thinking, teamwork, problem-solving skills, and an understanding of the challenges involved in future lunar exploration.

By combining NASA scientific resources with interactive gameplay, ORBY aims to turn complex space science concepts into an understandable and engaging learning experience.

projectDetails.name: Luminite
projectDetails.summary: Luminite is a geospatial dashboard designed to monitor and harmonize 25 years worth of hot spots data. Through the combination of MODIS and VIIRS’s archives, the platform eliminates duplicate sensor pings, mitigating alert fatigue. The interface features an interactive global map in conjunction with analytic graphs that evaluate fire activity yearly and monthly. Beyond this, Luminite incorporates behavioral anomaly detection to identify suspicious patterns such as odd thermal spikes indicating illegal land clearing.
projectDetails.details:
OVERVIEW

Luminite is a full-stack geo-analytical platform that processes, standardises, and visualises 25 years of global active wildfire data (2000–Present). By ingesting raw satellite telemetry, the application generates an interactive global wildfire calendar and a multi-layered global wildfire map.

How activity is counted: Each 0.1° grid cell counts once per day when fire is detected. This “cell-day” measure avoids inflating counts when VIIRS records several hotspots in an area where MODIS records one. We then adjust for the sensors’ remaining differences in detection sensitivity.

CORE

  • Data Pipeline (pipeline.py, archives.py): Ingests raw CSV data from NASA FIRMS, incorporating both scientific-quality historical archives (fire_archive_.csv) and near-real-time feeds (fire_nrt_.csv with a 3-hour latency) across four major satellite instruments: MODIS (Terra & Aqua, 2000–2025) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP from 2012, NOAA-20 from 2018).
  • Data Standardisation: Unifies column schemas, converts timestamps to UTC (observation_time_utc), normalises confidence ratings into Low, Nominal, and High levels, and standardises measurement units (e.g., frp to frp_mw, scan to scan_km).
  • Write-Validate-Publish Pattern: Protects against data corruption by staging outputs in data/staging/[run-id]. Automated validation checks ensure boundary compliance (Lat: -90 to 90, Long: -180 to 180), exact row counts, and correct data types, while recording SHA-256 hashes in catalog/manifest.json before atomic publishing via os.replace().
  • Historical Merging (merge.py): Combines overlapping datasets without double-counting by applying a strict historical cutoff (ARCHIVE_CUTOFF_YEAR = 2025). Uses hardlinks (os.link()) for hundreds of gigabytes of historical parquet files to grant instant access without physical duplication, with graceful fallback across filesystems.
  • Sensor Calibration & Harmonisation: Addresses the tripling of raw data cells caused by Suomi-NPP's 2012 launch (as VIIRS detects smaller and colder fires than MODIS). It calculates active 0.1-degree cell-days using bitmasks (terra=1, aqua=2, snpp=4, noaa20=8) and applies a spatial hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage (James-Stein) algorithm across 1-degree cells, 5-degree blocks, and global priors, validated via leave-one-year-out cross-validation.
  • Processing & Serving (api.py, build_web_data.py): Serialises data into Zstd-compressed, partitioned Parquet files (partitioned by dataset, year, and month) supporting column and partition pruning. Served via a high-performance FastAPI backend with embedded DuckDB or entirely client-side via DuckDB-WASM using HTTP range requests on static hosts (GitHub Pages/CDN).

STRENGTH

  • 25-Year Trend Analysis: Neutralises sensor sensitivity discrepancies to allow researchers and environmentalists to track long-term wildfire trends from 2000 onward without artificial spikes caused by technological upgrades.
  • Serverless Architecture: Spatial sorting of Parquet files enables DuckDB-WASM to power the entire frontend client-side, eliminating the need for a dedicated server.
  • Graceful Fallback & Data Integrity: Automatically returns NULL for regions lacking sufficient data points for stable calibration. Employs strict idempotency checks, checksums, and atomic publishing to prevent file corruption.
  • Multi-Resolution Visualisation: Offers seamless exploration across various scales, ranging from 2-degree JSON dot grids and 1/4 or 1/16 degree aggregated Parquet grids to Uber H3 spatial grids and individual fire detections.
  • Export & Advanced Analytics: Supports CSV data exports, canvas-based PNG map rendering, historical baseline comparisons, and statistical significance testing via the Seasonal Mann-Kendall test.

IMPACT

  • Empowering Researchers: Equips climate scientists, conservationists, and government agencies with unskewed historical data to study climate change, carbon emissions, and land-use changes.
  • Intuitive Accessibility: Translates complex satellite telemetry into an easy-to-understand interactive calendar and multi-source map leveraging WebGL, MapLibre GL JS, and Google Maps 3D.
  • Improved Emergency Response: Enables regional authorities and land managers to quickly identify wildfire season anomalies and deploy firefighting resources more effectively.

SYSTEM

  • Languages:
    • Python: Data pipeline orchestration, API development, spatial aggregation, and calibration engine.
    • JavaScript, HTML, CSS: Frontend application logic and UI components.
    • DuckDB & DuckDB-WASM: In-process analytical SQL database engine.
    • Pandas & PyArrow: Data cleaning, manipulation, and Parquet file handling.
    • Uber H3: Geospatial hexagonal gridding library.
    • FastAPI & Pydantic: Asynchronous REST API framework and data validation schemas with automated OpenAPI documentation.
    • MapLibre GL JS & WebGL: Rendering vector tiles, dark mode/satellite views, and a custom 3D globe using NASA Blue Marble textures.
    • Google Maps API: Optional 3D map layer.
    • Parquet & Zstd: Optimised columnar data formats for spatial sorting and compression.

FEATURES

  • Hierarchical Bayesian Shrinkage: Avoids blunt global multipliers that distort local patterns by implementing a multi-level James-Stein shrinkage model. This balances local data (1-degree), block data (5-degree), and global monthly data while stabilising noisy readings from oceans and low-activity zones.
  • Bitmask Constellation Tracking: Encodes satellites as powers of two (terra=1, aqua=2, snpp=4, noaa20=8) and computes bit_or(platform_bit) for every 0.1-degree cell-day, instantly revealing the precise combination of satellites that observed a given cell.
  • Serverless Parquet-over-HTTP Architecture: Bypasses traditional database clusters in favor of static hosting. By sorting data by tile and date within Parquet files, DuckDB-WASM can fetch exact byte ranges over HTTP, allowing a complex spatial database application to execute entirely within a browser or CDN.

CONSIDERATION

  • Sensor Discrepancies: Accounted for how technological improvements across satellite sensors introduce artificial trends, neutralizing this bias through a dedicated calibration pipeline.
  • Data Scarcity & Noise: Addressed potential data sparsity in remote areas and oceans—which causes unstable values—by implementing hierarchical shrinkage and cross-validated shrinkage parameters (k{5,20,80}).
  • File Size & Bandwidth Optimisation: Minimized bandwidth requirements by rounding coordinates to integers (lat_e5 = round(latitude * 1e5) for ~1m equatorial precision) and quantising Fire Radiative Power (frp_c).
  • Pipeline Idempotency: Integrated multiple safeguards to allow safe pipeline restarts, including file modification time checks (mtime), file size verification, and SHA-256 manifests.

projectDetails.name: QuickX
projectDetails.summary: Our project makes NASA’s SphereX all-sky survey data accessible to people who aren’t professional researchers. We built a prototype platform that simplifies SphereX’s raw spectral and imaging data into clear, browsable visualizations that anyone can explore without needing a background in astrophysics. The challenge is twofold: researchers need an easier way to sample and browse SphereX’s vast dataset, and the wider public — especially in Cambodia — often sees astronomy as distant, abstract, and too technical to approach. Our platform addresses both by pairing a simplified data browser for researchers with an intuitive interface designed for first-time learners. This matters because Cambodia currently has very limited exposure to space science education. By letting students interact directly with real NASA data in a simple, hands-on way, we hope to shift the belief that astronomy is “too complicated” into curiosity and confidence. We see this prototype as a starting point — a tool Cambodian youth can use to learn, and later use to inspire and teach the next generation.
projectDetails.details:
QuickX is an interactive web application designed to help users visually explore astronomical imagery and detect celestial movement in real time. Rather than requiring complex scientific software, QuickX makes analyzing real space data intuitive through four core features:

  • Blink/Flicker Comparison: The flagship feature of QuickX rapidly alternates between two photographs of the exact same region of the sky taken at different times. Because the human eye is naturally sensitive to motion, any moving celestial body—such as an asteroid, comet, or potentially undiscovered object (nicknamed "Planet X")—appears to visibly "jump" back and forth against the static background stars.
  • Timeline View: Users can scroll chronologically through photos of the same part of the sky over time and watch how it slowly changes.
  • Inspector Tool: Users can click on any point in a photo to see detailed information about that exact spot, including its wavelength and pixel data.
  • Object Search: Users can search for a specific star or object (like "Barnard’s Star") using its official name format (such as NED) and instantly see its photos and data.

Benefits QuickX drastically cuts down the time needed to browse astronomical data. It turns a process that traditionally requires technical training and patience into something visual and fast, allowing users to do quick sampling while making it approachable for students exploring the sky for the first time.

Intended Impact Our goal is to make real NASA data approachable for Cambodian students, who rarely get hands-on exposure to astronomy. By giving them a tool that feels more like a game than a research instrument, we hope to spark curiosity and show that space science is reachable—planting the seed for a future generation of Cambodian astronomers.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used To develop and host QuickX, our team used HTML, Python, OpenAI, Claude, Porkbun for web hosting, and AWS S3 for storage.

How QuickX Is Creative Instead of relying solely on complex algorithms or spreadsheets to find anomalies in space, QuickX modernizes the classic astronomical "blink comparator" technique—turning human visual perception into a discovery engine. By gamifying the search for moving objects in the sky, we transformed passive data viewing into an interactive "treasure hunt" where students can experience the thrill of spotting real cosmic motion with their own eyes.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Accessibility and User Experience: We designed a simple, intuitive interface so students with zero prior astronomy background can start exploring right away.
  • Speed and Performance: Astronomical images can be large, so we used Amazon S3 for fast cloud storage to ensure switching between sky photos happens smoothly without lag, which is essential for the Blink/Flicker effect to work.
  • Scientific Authenticity: While keeping the experience approachable and game-like, we ensured the tool uses real astronomical data, official naming formats (NED), and accurate wavelength and pixel inspection.

projectDetails.name: SaveEarth
projectDetails.summary:
SaveEarth is a crop and rotation advisor web tool/telegram bot for Cambodian smallholder farmers, built for NASA Space Apps 2026 (Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data). A farmer drops a pin on their plot and picks a goal: steady harvests, soil health, or a balance. SaveEarth then simulates nine crops, plus fallow, at that exact spot. It uses 40 years of NASA POWER weather, SMAP soil moisture and 250 m SoilGrids soil data.

There are currently two tools mode that farmer can use.

"Recommend" returns the three best wet and dry season rotations. "I choose" scores the farmer's own plan and flags risks. Every score breaks down into the five factors that we use to predict the crop rotations.

A companion Telegram bot is also developed along side the web tool. It uses the same API and a village-name lookup, so farmers can get advice in a chat app they already use, without the need to go onto a web tool that they might not be so keen of, as the web is intended to be more focus on licensing out to government and NGO as well as the private sector.

The reason we believe our project matters is that erratic rain and tired soils are making traditional planting plans fail. SaveEarth turn satellite data into plot-specific guidance that saves water and reduces crop losses
projectDetails.details:
SaveEarth is a crop rotation advisory web tool and Telegram bot developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data." In Cambodia, changing rainfall and tired soils cause traditional planting calendars to fail, leading to crop losses and income anxiety for smallholder farmers. SaveEarth turns 40 years of satellite data into simple, plot-specific guidance that helps farmers choose the best crops for their fields. The tool offers two modes: "Recommend," which suggests the top three seasonal crop rotations, and "I Choose," which tests the farmer's own crop plan against historical climate risks across nine local crops and seasonal fallow.
A farmer marks their field on the map or searches for their village in Telegram. The system first checks ESA WorldCover 10-meter satellite data in less than a millisecond to reject non-arable pixels. For farm plots, our engine combines 40 years of NASA POWER daily weather, SMAP soil moisture, SRTM 30-meter elevation, and SoilGrids data. It runs an FAO-56 daily water balance to calculate crop water deficits (ETa / ETm) and simulate historical yields across 40 climate years. The engine then calculates points for five factors (water, soil fit, resilience, water savings, and soil health) using the formula P = 100 * w * (2f - 1), where w is the farmer's goal weight and f is the factor score between 0 and 1. The factor points sum to a raw score S, which converts into an intuitive 0 to 100 percent match rating ((S + 100) / 2). Finally, a dynamic programming optimizer pairs the highest-scoring wet and dry season crops while adding nitrogen credits for legume rotations.
SaveEarth provides clear benefits for daily farming decisions. It removes uncertainty by turning complex satellite numbers into easy guidance, helping farmers feel confident during unpredictable seasons. It also gives farmers financial visibility before they plant, estimating profits and input costs like seeds, fuel, and fertilizer. In addition, it protects the soil by recommending legume crops like mung bean or soybean after rice, which naturally adds nitrogen back into the soil and lowers fertilizer costs.
The intended impact is to build long-term climate resilience and financial security for smallholder farming families in Cambodia. The tool warns farmers about local risks, such as flood-prone areas or salty coastal soils, preventing costly crop failure. Our two-part delivery model ensures wide adoption: rural farmers can get instant advice through Telegram without downloading new apps, while NGOs, agricultural cooperatives, and government extension teams can use the web map for regional planning.
We built SaveEarth with modern, lightweight technologies. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Leaflet for interactive maps. The backend uses Python and FastAPI with Rasterio, GDAL, and NumPy for fast raster lookups and calculations. We packaged the backend in Docker and host it on Render with satellite tiles saved locally on disk for fast responses. The frontend and Telegram bot run on Vercel, with Cron-job.org keeping the backend warm.
Our project is creative because it is built around local Cambodian conditions rather than generic global data. We calibrated crop yields using official statistics from Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF, CAS 2024), and we benchmarked crop prices with UN World Food Programme data from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX). Instead of only looking at one crop, SaveEarth recommends multi-season rotations that improve the soil over time. Providing this through Telegram makes advanced satellite insights accessible to rural farmers through an app they already use every day.
When considering NASA judging criteria, our team focused on local impact and farmer independence. We accounted for Cambodia's different farming zones, from the low plains to coastal areas, as well as the difference between rainfed and irrigated fields. Most importantly, SaveEarth acts as a supportive advisor rather than making decisions for farmers. It never forces a choice; it gives farmers the scientific evidence they need to make the best decisions for their own land and families.

projectDetails.name: FireWatch Cambodia - Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Hotspots for Fire Risk Prediction in the Future in Cambodia
projectDetails.summary: FireWatch Cambodia is a fire-monitoring and prediction web application developed to address NASA's challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. Using NASA's satellite observations from the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), we collect, process, and harmonize fire hotspot records to support more consistent fire monitoring across Cambodia. The platform visualizes historical fire activity, identifies seasonal patterns, and analyzes unusual hotspot activity. Building on this harmonized dataset, we developed and deployed a machine learning model to predict areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The results are presented through an interactive map, allowing users to explore historical hotspots and potential future risk areas. By going beyond the visualization of past fire events, FireWatch Cambodia demonstrates how combining NASA satellite data, data science, and machine learning can support forward-looking fire monitoring. This project aims to improve awareness of potential fire-risk areas, support environmental monitoring, and provide useful information for communities, researchers, and decision-makers in Cambodia.
projectDetails.details:
FireWatch Cambodia

1. Project Overview

FireWatch Cambodia is a satellite-based fire monitoring and prediction platform developed in response to NASA's challenge, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. The project aims to improve the understanding of fire activity across Cambodia by combining observations from two NASA satellite instruments: the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS).

These satellite systems provide valuable active fire observations, but their differences in spatial resolution and detection characteristics make direct comparison challenging. FireWatch Cambodia addresses this challenge by collecting, processing, and harmonizing their hotspot datasets into a more consistent data structure.

Beyond historical fire visualization, our project incorporates data science and machine learning to analyze historical fire activity and predict areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The results are presented through an interactive web application, allowing users to explore historical hotspots, understand fire patterns, and view predicted risk areas.

Our goal is to demonstrate how harmonized NASA satellite observations and machine learning can support more informed environmental monitoring and fire-risk assessment in Cambodia.

2. How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

2.1. Satellite Data Collection

The project uses active fire and hotspot observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). We collect data from two satellite instruments:

  • MODIS: Provides active fire observations with approximately 1 km spatial resolution.
  • VIIRS: Provides active fire observations with approximately 375 m spatial resolution for its standard 375 m active fire product.

The datasets contain information such as geographic coordinates, acquisition dates and times, confidence levels, and other fire-related attributes.

2.2. Data Cleaning and Harmonization

Since MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection characteristics, their observations cannot simply be treated as identical measurements.

Our data processing workflow includes:

  • Cleaning and standardizing the collected datasets.
  • Handling missing values and inconsistent data formats.
  • Standardizing relevant attributes and geographic information.
  • Comparing observations from MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Combining processed records into a structured master dataset.

This process provides a foundation for analyzing observations from both satellite systems together while retaining their original data sources.

2.3. Historical Fire Pattern Analysis

After harmonization, we analyze historical hotspot observations to understand fire activity across Cambodia.

The analysis focuses on:

  • Geographic distribution of fire hotspots.
  • Monthly and seasonal fire activity.
  • Changes in hotspot frequency over time.
  • Differences and similarities between MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Unusual increases in hotspot activity.

These analyses help identify recurring patterns and areas that may require closer monitoring. By examining historical observations across different locations and time periods, users can better understand how fire activity changes over time.

2.4. Machine Learning-Based Fire-Risk Prediction

One of the main innovations of FireWatch Cambodia is the integration of machine learning into the harmonized satellite data workflow. Instead of only displaying historical fire observations, we developed and deployed a machine learning model to estimate potential future fire-risk areas across Cambodia.

We implemented and compared three machine learning algorithms: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting. Based on validation performance, the Random Forest Classifier was selected as the final model because it achieved the highest Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve (PR-AUC) among the tested algorithms using the harmonized dataset.

The model uses historical fire-related features derived from the harmonized MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records. These include fire counts over the previous 3, 7, and 30 days, total and mean Fire Radiative Power (FRP) over the previous 7 days, nearby fire counts within neighboring grid cells, the number of days since the last detected fire, and temporal features such as the month and day of the year. For spatial analysis, Cambodia is divided into grid cells measuring 0.1° in both latitude and longitude, equivalent to approximately 11 km.

The model predicts the probability of at least one satellite-detected hotspot occurring in each grid cell within the following three days. The predicted probabilities are then converted into three fire-risk categories: Low, Medium, and High Risk. The classification threshold for Medium Risk is approximately 0.321, selected using the validation dataset, while High Risk is assigned to areas with predicted probabilities of 0.50 or higher. These prediction results are exported as GeoJSON grid polygons and integrated into the FireWatch Cambodia platform, allowing users to explore potential fire-risk areas alongside historical satellite observations.

To evaluate the model's predictive performance, we applied a time-based data split, using observations from 2020 to 2023 for training, 2024 for validation and model selection, and 2025 for independent testing. The final Random Forest model trained on the harmonized dataset achieved a Precision of 62.24%, Recall of 73.92%, F1-Score of 67.58%, PR-AUC of 0.7410, ROC-AUC of 0.9421, and Brier Score of 0.0571 on the 2025 test set. The results also showed improvements in PR-AUC and F1-Score compared with the corresponding MODIS-only and VIIRS-only Random Forest experiments, demonstrating the potential benefits of combining observations from both satellite sensors.

The predictions represent estimated probabilities of future satellite-detected hotspots rather than guaranteed fire occurrences.

2.5. Interactive Web Application

FireWatch Cambodia presents the processed data and analytical results through an interactive web application.

Its main features include:

  • Interactive geographic visualization of fire hotspots.
  • Display of MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Visualization of harmonized fire data.
  • Historical fire activity analysis.
  • Machine learning-based future fire-risk predictions.

The application connects data processing, analysis, and prediction in one platform, making satellite-derived information easier to explore and understand.

Users can examine historical hotspot distributions and view predicted risk categories on a geographic map. This helps make complex satellite observations and analytical outputs more accessible to people who may not have technical experience in satellite data processing.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

FireWatch Cambodia aims to provide several benefits:

Improved Satellite Data Integration: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS observations helps address differences between the two datasets and supports more consistent fire monitoring. Instead of examining each satellite source separately, users can explore information from both systems through a unified platform.

Better Understanding of Fire Patterns: Historical analysis helps users explore where and when fire activity occurs across Cambodia. Geographic and seasonal analysis can reveal recurring patterns and changes in hotspot activity over time.

Forward-Looking Risk Assessment: Machine learning predictions extend the platform beyond historical monitoring by identifying areas with potentially higher future fire risk. This provides an additional perspective for understanding possible future hotspot activity.

Accessible Data Visualization: The interactive map makes complex satellite observations and analytical results easier to interpret. Bringing historical observations and predicted risk areas together helps users explore fire-related information in one place.

Environmental Awareness and Decision Support: The platform aims to provide useful information for researchers, environmental organizations, communities, and decision-makers working on fire monitoring and environmental protection.

Long-Term Intended Impact: Our long-term goal is to support more informed fire prevention and preparedness in Cambodia. We hope that the information provided by FireWatch Cambodia can help relevant stakeholders understand fire patterns, identify areas that may require closer attention, and support future environmental protection efforts.

4. Data Science Results and Evaluation

Our data science workflow produces several analytical outputs:

  1. Separate processed MODIS and VIIRS datasets.
  2. Pairwise comparison and matching results between satellite observations.
  3. A harmonized master dataset.
  4. Historical geographic and temporal fire activity analysis.
  5. Machine learning-based future fire-risk predictions.

These outputs were used to analyze historical fire activity across different geographic areas and time periods, as well as to develop a machine learning model for predicting potential future fire-risk areas.

The results were evaluated from two aspects: data harmonization and machine learning performance. The harmonization process was assessed by examining the consistency of satellite observations, the geographic matching between MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, and the differences in their fire detection characteristics.

For machine learning, the selected Random Forest model was evaluated using an independent test dataset from 2025. The evaluation metrics included Precision (62.24%), Recall (73.92%), F1-score (67.58%), PR-AUC (0.7410), ROC-AUC (0.9421), and Brier Score (0.0571).

These metrics provide an assessment of the model's ability to identify potential fire-risk areas and distinguish between grid cells with and without future hotspot activity. The comparison with MODIS-only and VIIRS-only experiments also helps demonstrate the potential value of combining observations from both satellite sensors.

5. Tools and Technologies

The project combines data science, satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, and web development.

Area Tools and Technologies

Satellite data NASA FIRMS, MODIS, VIIRS

Data processing Python, Pandas, NumPy

Geospatial analysis GeoPandas,

Data visualization Matplotlib, Plotly

Machine learning Logistic Regression, Random Forest, HistGradientBoosting

Frontend React, Vite, TypeScript

Backend Python, FastAPI

Database PostgreSQL

Deployment Vercel (frontend), Render (backend and database)

Development Environment and Hardware: The project was developed using standard computer equipment and software development environments. Cloud-based deployment services were used to make the web application accessible online. No specialized satellite hardware was required because the project uses publicly available satellite observations provided through NASA FIRMS.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of FireWatch Cambodia lies in connecting two different NASA satellite observation systems with historical data analysis and machine learning in a single platform.

Rather than treating MODIS and VIIRS as separate sources or simply displaying historical hotspots, our project develops a workflow that harmonizes their observations and uses the resulting data to support future fire-risk prediction.

Another important aspect is the integration of machine learning predictions directly into an interactive geographic platform. Users can explore both historical hotspot observations and predicted future risk areas, making the results more understandable and useful for environmental monitoring.

This combination of satellite data harmonization, data science, machine learning, and interactive visualization creates a more comprehensive approach to understanding fire activity in Cambodia.

7. Limitations and Future Development

Although FireWatch Cambodia provides historical fire monitoring and machine learning-based risk predictions, several improvements can strengthen the platform in the future.

Potential developments include:

  • Improving model performance through additional historical and environmental variables.
  • Conducting further validation using independent fire observations.
  • Improving spatial and temporal prediction resolution.
  • Integrating additional environmental data, such as rainfall, temperature, vegetation, and land-cover information.
  • Connect with real time dataset of the fire from NASA
  • Developing an operational alert mechanism for relevant communities and authorities.

These improvements could help transform FireWatch Cambodia into a more comprehensive fire-risk monitoring and decision-support system.

8. Conclusion

FireWatch Cambodia demonstrates how NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations can be harmonized and enhanced through data science and machine learning. By integrating historical fire analysis, future fire-risk prediction, and interactive visualization, the project goes beyond simply showing where fires have been detected in the past.

Through its interactive platform, users can explore satellite observations, understand historical fire patterns, and examine areas with potentially higher future fire risk. The project brings together satellite data processing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, and web development to make complex fire-related information more accessible.

Ultimately, FireWatch Cambodia aims to make satellite-derived fire information more accessible and useful, contributing to improved environmental monitoring and a better understanding of potential fire risks across Cambodia. We hope this project can provide a foundation for future fire-risk assessment, environmental awareness, and more informed decision-making.

projectDetails.name: CAMFarm
projectDetails.summary:
CAMFarm helps Cambodian farmers with limited budgets check planting conflicts and potential water shortfalls before buying seeds after harvest. The web prototype combines five complete years of NASA POWER rainfall history with farmer-entered location, previous crop, soil texture, drainage, irrigation access, and planting month to compare soybean, groundnut, maize, and paddy rice. Transparent rules flag crop-family repetition and waterlogging risks from poor drainage, explaining each option’s advantages and constraints.

Users can inspect historical rainfall against FAO crop water-use ranges, compare crops side by side, save plans in their browser, and download comparison data. SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS, and ECOSTRESS provide supplementary observations or coverage when available; GRACE and SRTM are not integrated.

Built with React, TypeScript, CSS, Vite/Vinext, and Cloudflare Workers, CAMFarm aims to help farmers identify unsuitable planting choices before committing money. It remains an exploratory prototype that does not forecast weather or guarantee harvest outcomes, and its intended benefits have not yet been measured in farmer trials.
projectDetails.details:
After a harvest, Cambodian farmers face a big decision: what should they plant next, and what risks should they check before buying seeds? We built CAMFarm to help answer that. It’s a web prototype that evaluates soybean, groundnut, maize, and paddy rice by combining NASA rainfall data with the farmer's own field knowledge.


Instead of just giving a generic recommendation, the app connects regional satellite observations with on-the-ground reality. A farmer inputs their location, previous crop, soil texture, drainage, irrigation setup, and planting time. CAMFarm then runs this through a set of hardcoded rules to flag crop-family repetition, drainage issues, and potential water shortages.
We designed the output to show the why behind every option. For example, if a farmer reports poor drainage, the app throws a waterlogging warning for upland crops. If they have heavy clay, it adds a specific caution against groundnuts. Users can dig into each crop's details, save their plans locally in the browser, and download side-by-side comparisons.
To power the environmental context, we pull the last five years of historical precipitation and temperature data using NASA POWER (our default Mondulkiri example uses 2021–2025 data). We map this against FAO crop water-use guidelines to help visualize possible water shortfalls. The app’s observation workspace also pulls in SMAP surface soil moisture, MODIS vegetation greenness, and GPM IMERG rainfall when available, along with ECOSTRESS coverage. These satellite sources act as extra context rather than strict ranking factors, and the UI is careful to point out when data is missing or just showing coverage rather than numerical values.


Under the hood, the app is built with React, TypeScript, and CSS, bundled with Vite/Vinext, and runs on Cloudflare Workers (published via ChatGPT Sites). We used ChatGPT and Codex to speed up the coding and UI design, generated the botanical illustrations with AI, and put our presentation together in Canva.


Right now, CAMFarm is very much an exploratory prototype. We're clear in the app that historical rainfall isn't a forecast, and it doesn't directly measure the water actually reaching the roots. There is still a lot of local reality to account for—like specific crop varieties, pests, soil chemistry, and market prices. Before we make any hard claims about boosting yields or saving water, the next step is getting it into the hands of farmers for real-world agronomic testing.
